title: Rep. Nancy Mace Secures Major South Carolina Wins As House Passes Water Infrastructure Bill
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. (Sept. 16, 2026) – Congresswoman Nancy Mace announced today the House passed the Water Resources Development Act (WRDA) of 2026, delivering critical water infrastructure, flood protection, and water supply investments to South Carolina.

Mace secured multiple South Carolina priorities in the legislation, including water and wastewater infrastructure in Hilton Head Island, Isle of Palms, Berkeley County, and Beaufort, as well as expanded authorizations for projects tied to Lakes Marion and Moultrie. This totals $100 million in authorized funding for water and wastewater infrastructure in the Lowcountry. The legislation also delivers for Charleston by integrating coastal storm risk management and tidal and inland flood management.

“South Carolina is the fastest-growing state in the country, and our infrastructure needs to keep pace,” said Congresswoman Mace. “We made sure South Carolina’s priorities were front and center in WRDA, from stronger water and wastewater systems to better flood protection and infrastructure built for growth. These investments will make a real difference for families, businesses, and communities across the Lowcountry. This is what putting South Carolina first looks like.”

The South Carolina priorities secured by Mace include:

$10,000,000 authorized for water and wastewater infrastructure, including stormwater management, in the town of Hilton Head Island, SC.

$10,000,000 authorized for water and wastewater infrastructure, including stormwater management, in the city of Isle of Palms, SC.

$14,000,000 authorized for water and wastewater infrastructure, including water supply and distribution systems, in Berkeley County, SC.

$60,000,000 increase in authorization for wastewater treatment and water supply treatment and distribution projects related to Lakes Marion and Moultrie, SC.

$6,000,000 authorized for water and wastewater infrastructure, including water supply and distribution systems, in the City of Beaufort, SC.

Modification of the project for coastal storm risk management in the Charleston Peninsula, SC, to include features for tidal- and inland-related flood risk management measures.

Deauthorization of Tidewater Reach section of the Charleston Harbor navigation system (adjacent to the Union Pier Terminal). title: Congressman Mackenzie Applauds Passage of Ratepayer Protection Act
text:
Washington, D.C. — Congressman Ryan Mackenzie (PA-07), representing the Lehigh Valley and the Poconos, applauded the passage of the Ratepayer Protection Act on Tuesday evening. This bipartisan legislation, which the Congressman has co-sponsored, requires data centers and other large energy consumers to pay their fair share for the cost of the new energy infrastructure they necessitate.

According to the U.S. Department of Energy, data centers currently account for roughly 4.4% of U.S. electricity consumption, a figure projected to increase to between 6.7% and 12% by 2028 as AI computing capacity continues to grow. Many new AI data centers require 100 megawatts (MW) or more of electricity, enough to power tens of thousands of homes, and often necessitate costly investments in new generation, transmission, and distribution infrastructure.

The Ratepayer Protection Act maintains local control and would require new large electricity customers with a peak demand of at least 100 megawatts to pay the full cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrades needed to serve their facilities, rather than shifting those costs to existing ratepayers. It also requires these customers to provide financial assurances before utilities begin construction, ensuring the utility can recover its investment even if the customer later ends service.

“Communities in the Lehigh Valley and the Poconos should not be footing the energy bill for data centers they never asked for,” said Congressman Ryan Mackenzie. “When companies want to build facilities that require major upgrades to energy infrastructure, they should be the ones who pay. The bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act, which I’ve co-sponsored, will help to ensure that data centers and similar facilities pay their fair share of the costs they produce instead of passing them on to local residents.”

title: Magaziner Bill to Require Civil Liberties Training for DHS Intelligence Employees Passes U.S. House of Representatives
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – The U.S. House of Representatives today passed U.S. Representative Seth Magaziner's Department of Homeland Security Intelligence and Analysis Training Act, legislation that will require training for intelligence employees at the Department of Homeland Security on civil rights, civil liberties and privacy protections.

The legislation establishes a formal training curriculum for employees of the DHS Office of Intelligence and Analysis (I&A), which is responsible for collecting, analyzing, and sharing intelligence with state, local, Tribal, territorial, and private-sector partners to help protect the American people from threats to public safety.

“Under the Trump Administration, the Department of Homeland Security has shown a willful disregard for the privacy and civil liberties of the American people,” said Magaziner. “This legislation is a small but important step toward reining in the lawless behavior by federal agents, and protecting the American people from federal overreach.”

Passage of Magaziner's legislation follows numerous examples of violations of civil liberties by the Department of Homeland Security during the second Trump Administration.

During Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis from December 2025 to February 2026, undercover federal agents infiltrated meetings at a public library and a church, wore wires to record conversations, and ran license plates at an anti-ICE gathering to compile dossiers on attendees, prompting a federal class action alleging violations of the First and Fourth Amendments.

Separately, DHS used an obscure customs statute to obtain YouTube account records forjournalists covering immigration enforcement, after a judge had already rejected search warrants for the same accounts for lack of probable cause. Meanwhile, the internal watchdog charged with checking abuses like these, DHS's Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties, was dismantled in March 2025, leaving the department with diminished oversight even as these incidents occurred.

Having passed the House, the bill now heads to the Senate for consideration.

This is the first bill Magaziner has passed through the House as standalone legislation. He previously passed 13 amendments to other pieces of legislation, secured funding for30 earmarks, and attached his bill to help the seafood industry better market scup as part of the FY2026 Agriculture Appropriations Act.

title: Malliotakis Bill to Protect Taxpayers from Ghost Preparers Passes House Unanimously
text:
(WASHINGTON, DC) — Congresswoman Nicole Malliotakis applauded the unanimous House passage of her legislation, H.R. 9499, the Protecting Taxpayers from Ghost Preparers Act. This legislation takes an important step to ensure that taxpayers who are victims of preparer fraud are not unfairly punished for actions they did not commit.

Under current law, when a dishonest tax preparer commits fraud without the taxpayer's knowledge, the taxpayer may be subject to an indefinite statute of limitations, even if they had no intent to evade their tax obligations. The bill addresses this gap in the law by clarifying that the unlimited statute of limitations for fraudulent tax returns applies only when the taxpayer intended to commit fraud—not when a dishonest tax preparer acted alone without the taxpayer's knowledge.

Several recent New York cases underscore how dishonest tax preparers can exploit taxpayers and defraud the system. An individual on Long Island pleaded guilty to a nearly $12 million tax fraud scheme. They prepared fraudulent tax returns, charged clients more than $1 million in fees—including a percentage of their refunds—and put those taxpayers at risk while enriching themselves. An individual in the Bronx was sentenced to four years in prison for orchestrating a decade-long, $145 million tax fraud scheme. He oversaw the filing of tens of thousands of false tax returns, generating approximately $12 million in fraudulent proceeds.

“Far too many taxpayers have been forced to spend months trying to fix IRS problems they did not create, and my office has seen that frustration firsthand through more than 1,400 IRS-related constituent cases,” said Congresswoman Nicole Malliotakis. “With the unanimous passage of my legislation in the House, we are one step closer to ensuring innocent taxpayers are not penalized for fraud or misconduct committed by a tax preparer. This bill puts the responsibility where it belongs—on those who break the law—and gives taxpayers greater protection when they have acted in good faith. I hope the Senate will now take up this bipartisan, commonsense measure and send it to the President’s desk.”

“Shady businesses that file tax returns on behalf of taxpayers but deceive the IRS by making it appear that the taxpayer prepared the return are not just committing fraud – they are committing a crime that could leave an innocent taxpayer facing consequences and potential IRS penalties for something they did not do,” said Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith (MO-08). “With the Protecting Taxpayers from Ghost Preparers Act, we can ensure taxpayers do not face an indefinite future of IRS assessments or penalties due to the misdeeds of others. Having seen the impact of tax fraud on victims in the communities she serves, Representative Malliotakis is protecting the rights of taxpayers by keeping the IRS focused on going after the criminals responsible.”

title: Representative John W. Mannion’s (NY-22) Legislation to Improve Reading Outcomes in Elementary and Secondary Schools Passes House With Bipartisan Support
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. - Representative John W. Mannion (NY-22) today announced that his legislation, the Science of Reading Act of 2026, passed the U.S. House of Representatives with bipartisan support. The bipartisan bill, also supported by Representative Erin Houchin (IN-9) and Representative Kevin Kiley (CA-3), aims to strengthen reading outcomes by promoting evidence-based instruction grounded in the Science of Reading.

Representative John W. Mannion said, “As a teacher for nearly three decades - and the husband of a literacy expert - I know that strong reading skills are the foundation for success in the classroom, in the workplace, and throughout life. The Science of Reading Act gives teachers and students access to proven, evidence-based approaches that help kids become stronger readers. I’m proud that Republicans and Democrats came together to pass this legislation and move us one step closer to improving reading outcomes for students in NY-22 and across the country. Strong schools and strong readers are essential to America’s ability to compete and win globally.”

Representative Erin Houchin said, “Reading is the foundation of learning, and we cannot accept declining literacy rates as the status quo. The Science of Reading Act will equip classrooms with proven methods to ensure every student can read. Indiana has shown that the Science of Reading works, and I’m proud to see this important legislation pass the House.”

The Science of Reading Act would amend the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965 to require that literacy instruction funded through the Comprehensive Literacy State Development (CLSD) program follows the “science of reading.” Furthermore, the bill would limit the use of the three‑cueing model as the primary model of instruction for states participating in this program. This bill also carefully ensures protections for individualized instructional supports for students with disabilities and English language learners.

The science of reading uses five evidence-based components of phonemic awareness - phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension - to teach students literacy skills. More than 40 states have implemented these methods successfully, helping to create more consistent and comprehensive outcomes for students.

title: Rep. McBride Calls on Speaker Johnson to Keep House in Session, Address AI Risks
text:
WASHINGTON, DC — U.S. Representative Sarah McBride (D-Del.) joined her Democratic colleagues in calling on Speaker of the House Mike Johnson to keep the House in session until Congress takes immediate and meaningful action to address the risks posed by artificial intelligence. Speaker Johnson previously canceled the House’s final two weeks of scheduled votes in September and canceled the House’s remaining votes this week today, sending members home early.

The letter comes amid growing warnings from AI industry leaders and researchers about the risks associated with rapidly advancing AI models. Rep. McBride recently released a statement calling on Congress to act, warning that no concentration of such power — whether in an individual, a company, a nation, or a technology — can be allowed to go unchecked, unrestrained, or unregulated.

Rep. McBride said:

“AI presents potentially the biggest change for humanity since human beings went from nomadic creatures to stationary, community-based societies.

“Whether you think AI will be a fountain of youth or a doomsday technology or something in between, its power - both present and potential - is indisputable. Its capacity to cure diseases or produce bioweapons, to protect against the most advanced cyberattacks or hack the most robust technological fortresses, to foster shared prosperity for the many or to amass unimaginable wealth for the few, are each different sides of the same coin: significant capacity that can lead to superhuman power.

“No concentration of such power - whether it be in an individual, a company, a nation, or a technology - can be allowed to go unchecked or unrestrained. And it certainly cannot go unregulated.

“Since I entered Congress, I’ve been calling on my colleagues to meet this moment and to marshal our collective power to regulate AI. It’s why, as a member of the Science, Space, and Technology Committee, I’m pushing for regulations domestically and, as a member of the Foreign Affairs Committee, I’ve argued for an 'arms control' approach to AI globally. We need human-centric laws that protect our economy, our finances, our privacy, our health, our democracy, and, yes, our existence. We need national and international action. We need it now.

“For AI to have any good, we must protect against its harm. And the clock is ticking. As we’ve seen with other technologies, the longer we wait, the harder it becomes. We cannot feel too much urgency. We cannot be too imaginative. There is simply no realistic risk in today’s politics that we do too much. The risk is that we do too little – and that is a risk that is simply too great to bear.

“Whistleblowers are warning us. AI CEOs are requesting it. And the people are demanding it. Congress should not leave until we’ve fulfilled our responsibility to our constituents and to humanity. Future generations expect nothing less.”

In the letter, Rep. McBride and her colleagues underscore the urgency of the moment and call on the House to remain in session until Congress advances meaningful, bipartisan safeguards for AI.

“We write to urge you to keep the House of Representatives in session to enable Congress to take urgent action to address the catastrophic risks posed by advanced artificial intelligence. Those risks take any of several forms, separately and in combination—of agentic misalignment, mass cybersecurity breaches, and development of biological or chemical weapons. Reasonable minds may disagree about precisely how Congress should regulate this rapidly evolving technology. We cannot disagree about the imperative for Congress to act. Instead of action, you have announced vacation. After a month-long August recess, the House leadership changed the schedule to announce two more weeks of vacation–immediately prior to yet another month of recess in October,” wrote the lawmakers.

The letter points to several recent developments and warnings from AI researchers and industry leaders, including:

An incident involving Hugging Face in which OpenAI models undergoing cybersecurity evaluations caused swarms of agents that circumvented controls designed to isolate them from the internet, exploited vulnerabilities, hacked third-party systems, and altered evidence of their activity;

More than 1,300 top employees of frontier AI companies calling on the U.S. government to support an international effort to develop tools that can “deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development”; and

Cases disrupted by Anthropic in which researchers used Claude for biological research that could have aided the development of biological weapons.

Despite these warnings, Speaker Johnson is sending lawmakers home today, and the House will remain out of session until November.

“Whether with these proposals or any other variants, AI experts and leading companies agree that the United States can lead the world in artificial intelligence while establishing reasonable safeguards that protect Americans and our national security. We can—and must—do both. While AI safety experts and Americans increasingly urge action to confront this conflagration of risk, Congress fiddles…After next week, the House resumes its vacation—for another six weeks,” the lawmakers said.

Rep. McBride has been working to both harness the potential and mitigate the risks of AI since coming to Congress. As a member of the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee, she has pushed for a federal framework for AI and, as a member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has argued for an "arms control" approach to AI globally. She also introduced the READ AI Models Act, bipartisan legislation aimed at increasing transparency around AI models.

“The House should remain in session until Congress advances meaningful, bipartisan AI safeguards,” the lawmakers concluded.

title: Rep. McBride Secures Delaware Priorities in Water Resources Development Act
text:
WASHINGTON, DC — Today, U.S. Representative Sarah McBride (D-Del.) voted to pass the Water Resources Development Act (WRDA), which includes several Delaware priorities she advocated for during the development of the legislation. WRDA authorizes critical water resources infrastructure projects and studies through the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Civil Works Program, supporting flood and storm protection, ports and harbors, and inland waterway navigation across the country.

As the state with the lowest mean elevation in the country, Delaware faces significant risks from flooding, coastal storms, and shoreline erosion. WRDA is a critical tool for strengthening Delaware’s water infrastructure, protecting communities across the state, and preparing coastal communities in Sussex County and communities along the Delaware River for future flooding.

“Protecting Delaware from flooding and extreme weather starts with ensuring our water infrastructure is built to withstand the challenges of today and tomorrow,” said Rep. McBride. “I’m proud that the House version of the bill, which passed with bipartisan support, includes several priorities I fought to secure for Delaware — strengthening protections along the Delaware River, advancing flood mitigation in New Castle and along the Assawoman Canal, and increasing support for the Delaware River Basin. WRDA isn’t just an investment in our water infrastructure — it’s an investment in our economy, our communities, and the future of our state.”

Delaware priorities secured by Rep. McBride include:

Advancing flood and shoreline protection along the Delaware River by authorizing a study focused on flood risk management, shoreline damage prevention and mitigation, recreation, and ecosystem restoration;

Supporting flood mitigation in the City of New Castle by authorizing a flood-risk-management study;

Exploring additional flood protections for the Assawoman Canal through a newly authorized study; and

Strengthening support for water infrastructure across the Delaware River Basin by expanding an existing environmental infrastructure program to cover the entire Basin and increasing its authorization from $20 million to $92.69 million.

The bill now heads to the U.S. Senate.

title: Chairman Emeritus McCaul Discusses Evolutions in Counterterrorism 25 Years After 9/11 at CHS Hearing
text:
WASHINGTON – At today's House Homeland Security Committee hearing, Congressman Michael McCaul (R-Texas) — chairman emeritus and current vice chair of the committee — spoke with DC Fire and EMS Department Chief John Donnelly, FDNY Chief of Fire Prevention Thomas Currao, and Chief Secretary Officer for the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey Greg Ehrie.

They discussed the strides made in protecting Americans from terrorism 25 years after 9/11 and the need to continuously adapt and innovate our technologies. Rep. McCaul also asked the witnesses about the evolving aviation threat posed by modern drones.

Image

Click to watch

Full Exchange:

McCaul: You know, I vividly remember that day as we all do. Horrific day. For us, it's living history. For many now, it's textbook history in the schools. After 9/11, I became the Chief of Counterterrorism and National Security in the Western District of Texas. I became a student of counterterrorism, and then became chairman of this committee. [I] worked very closely with NYPD and the New York Fire Department as well.

I remember [in] 1993, we had a pre-warning: Ramzi Yousef trying to bring down the World Trade Center. And it was originally a plot to hit 12 synagogues simultaneously, symbolizing the 12 tribes of Israel. He modified his plan to take down the symbol of economic power, the World Trade Center, one pillar, one building toppling over the other. As you all know, he came actually relatively close to achieving that goal if the bomb had gone off closer to one of the pillar beams.

But then he escapes, meets with his uncle Khalid Sheikh Mohammed. He develops the Bojinka plot. I knew the Diplomatic Security Corps officer who arrested him, and eerily, they found baby dolls in his apartment stuffed with chemical explosives to [bring] onto airplanes to blow them up. The Bojinka plot also being 12 airliners, symbolic of the 12 tribes of Israel. He conspires with Khalid Sheikh Mohammed on 9/11.

The idea that planes could be turned into suicide missions was something that was not imaginable, and it was a failure of imagination. We saw planes hijacked, but not turned into cruise missiles targeted at buildings. In this case, three symbols of power: economic, military, and what in Arabic [is] called the building of laws, which was the United States Capitol.

The threat was aviation then. I believe it's also aviation today. I chaired the special events task force on the FIFA games, and the number one focus [was] drones and the impact that drones could have. I just got back from Ukraine, saw the amazing drone capabilities they've developed in this war against Russia, this conflict. But the modern aviation threat 25 years later is my question for the three of you.

We worked very hard, and the chairman passed the Safer Skies Act to help federal, state, and local to protect these events. But I'd like for the three of you to comment now on what I consider to be an old threat being aviation, but in a more modern capacity, and that is the threat of drones. Perhaps I could start with Chief Donnelly and work my way through.

Donnelly: Drones bring a new threat to us, and we don't clearly understand it—meaning the evolution of drones and what their capabilities really are and really aren't leaves us in a spot where it's hard to prepare. We are preparing that these weapons can do things in our community that could be delivered by a car or by some other method, so we prepare [for] that. I think the second part of the challenge is awareness of drones.

As you know here in the District of Columbia, the airspace is extremely restricted, and any drone that's up should be official. But sometimes there's so many different agencies with them up here, it takes a while to sort out whether or not it's an official one. And that isn't a local thing, that's a federal thing. That's all the different federal agencies putting them up. So here in the district, we are working with our partners in the Secret Service, with Capitol Police, with the Metropolitan Police Department.

McCaul: Well, you have a lot of federal buildings, including the United States Capitol. I know there are federal agencies assigned to that, but I do think coordination, like with the Safer Skies Act, the intent behind that should apply.

Donnelly: Yeah, and that's where we want to be. We want to be coordinated so that when a drone's up, we know if it's good or bad. I'm confident that we can respond to the threats that they bring, but the coordination, the awareness of what their real capabilities are would be helpful.

McCaul: Thanks. Chief Currao?

Currao: Thank you very much for the question. First of all, thank you for the support. It was grant funding that allowed the FDNY to really build a very robust drone and robotics program. It is a program that's come to quite significant fruition. We use it a lot in our fire and rescue operations in a marine environment.

And we have actually been a leader working with a lot of our counterparts to actually develop policy. I think from our perspective, our biggest concern is the threat of even just a drone over a special event, over a large area, mass panic. We readily identify—you mentioned Ukraine—that these, uh, drones can be weaponized, and we're concerned about chemicals, biologicals, other dispersion methods.

And I agree with Chief Donnelly, we're still trying to understand what is the real threat vector, right? How effective would it be? But in many ways, I’m very concerned about the fact that we could have a mass panic situation at something like the New York City Marathon, [or] any of those particular areas.

McCaul: Or the Boston Marathon.

Currao: Boston Marathon, absolutely.

McCaul: And by the way, Firehouse 10 is the most dramatic experience, and seeing the flag that flew on 9/11 just always blows me away when I see it. But, Mr. Ehrie?

Ehrie: No, sir, I agree with your assessment. We, like my colleagues, we’re watching this, and the technology is outstripping our ability to identify and mitigate the technology. And certainly what we're seeing over in Ukraine is the perfection of drone warfare, and that can be extended out across the full spectrum of threats we're going to face, everywhere from criminal, a delivery system, all the way up to a catastrophic counterterrorism attack.

As you well know from your work with FIFA, it was our biggest fear that there was going to be something that came out in a drone that we could not either identify, and we certainly have a very limited capacity to mitigate that threat if we did identify it. Uh, as the chairman asked, we are extremely near [the]aviation industry, [you] see this over the airports. It was years ago in Scotland that a drone basically parked itself over the airfield, didn't do anything, but it stopped all transportation. The airport had to shut down.

That threat is still existent today. We would not have a way to take that drone down unless it was a kinetic piece, so we're working very closely. If there's something this committee could do, especially on the federal level, a regulation they could put out there, but we need to identify the right technologies to counter this threat.

title: McCaul on House Floor: "Evil Is on the March. History Is Calling. Now Is the Time to Act."
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Emeritus Michael McCaul (R-Texas) delivered opening remarks on the House floor in support of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which he introduced in the House with Congressman Steny Hoyer (D-Md.) and a bipartisan group of their colleagues.

Image

Click to watch

Remarks as delivered:

This is a critical time in history — a time my friend Senator Lindsey Graham described as a “magic moment," a moment that we cannot afford to waste.

America’s adversaries — Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea — are working together to threaten the free world. And make no mistake: they are watching what we do here and now today, because they know they will suffer if this bill is passed.

Senator Lindsey Graham understood these global threats well. That’s why we spent more than a year working on this bill. He brought Republicans and Democrats together and secured the White House’s support. Today, we have a chance to finish his work — to help end this war in Europe and to project peace through strength around the globe.

I’m proud to champion the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, and I want to thank Mr. Hoyer and our colleagues on both sides of the aisle for their strong support.

For me, this is also personal. Lindsey Graham was my friend and my mentor. We shared a fundamental belief: “America is strongest at home when it projects strength abroad.”

This legislation does exactly that.

It targets the money that fuels Russia’s war machine. It sanctions Russian officials and oligarchs, banks and financial institutions, and the shadow fleet that helps [keep] cheap Russian energy moving.

And through precisely-targeted tariffs, it also punishes countries providing financial support for the deadliest war in Europe since WWII.

Why? Because, as we’ve heard from President Zelensky’s team, you can evade sanctions — which the Russians have done for years — but you cannot evade tariffs.

In fact, President Zelenksy’s sanctions expert, whom I personally met with in Kyiv, told me: “Tariffs are a powerful way to amplify the impact of sanctions.”

That’s why they are the teeth of this bill. Pursuant to the bill’s rule of construction, only the top five importers of Russian oil will be tariffed, and if a country falls off of the top five list, the tariffs are removed. It incentivizes a race to the bottom.

These countries have a choice to make about whether they will continue to sustain Putin’s aggression. Putin believes he can keep financing this war indefinitely. We need to change that calculation — and bleed his regime economically dry.

Because the Kremlin has murdered thousands of civilians in cold blood. They’ve bombed sacred churches and schools. They’ve kidnapped countless children, tortured and indoctrinated them, and sent them to fight on the frontlines against their own country.

We have a moral responsibility to bring an end to this suffering. But this is also a matter of national security.

If Putin is rewarded for invading a sovereign nation — if he succeeds — he has already told us he will go further. His army will move into Moldova, Georgia, and the Baltic States. Just like Putin wants to bring back the power of the Soviet Union, President Xi wants to restore imperial China. These dictators must be deterred — before it’s too late.

This legislation also extends sanctions on Iran, which are set to expire at the end of this year. Again, this is all tied together. In 2024, I spoke about the Iranian drones being used by Russia to kill Ukrainians. In return, Russia is reportedly providing targeting information to the IRGC.

We cannot look at one part of this threat and ignore the others. This bill leverages our economic strength to make it harder for these regimes to finance aggression.

Lindsey Graham once said that this bill would be his greatest achievement. I can think of no better way, Mr. Speaker, to honor his life and legacy than by passing these tough sanctions, which will force Mr. Putin to the negotiating table.

Evil is on the march. History is calling. And now is the time to act

title: McCaul on House Floor: "A Vote Against This Bill Is a Vote for Putin and His Unholy Alliance."
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Emeritus Michael McCaul (R-Texas) delivered closing remarks on the House floor in support of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which he introduced in the House with Congressman Steny Hoyer (D-Md.) and a bipartisan group of their colleagues.

Image

Click to watch

Remarks as delivered:

Let me just say, I was at the Ukraine embassy last night, and when I announced to them that the rule had passed to allow this bill to go to the floor for final passage, I got a standing ovation — standing ovation from the ambassador and all supporters of Ukraine.

When I chaired the Foreign Affairs Committee, I often said, "Partisanship stops at the water’s edge." I still believe that. Mr. Meeks and I did pass the emergency wartime supplemental bill that gave Ukraine a lifeline to prevent occupation from Russia so they could advance in their drone technology.

But I’m a bit disheartened by some of my colleagues’ remarks here today because they don’t reflect that principle. In fact, [their arguments are] all about the president; it's false arguments about expansion of tariff authorities, when [the tariffs are] actually limited to our adversaries buying energy from Russia. Their premise is: "We don't like the president, so let's just do nothing." Let's do nothing as we go into the wintertime, when we know the fighting will intensify.

We don't have time to wait; Ukraine doesn't have time to wait. That's precisely why President Zelensky told me when I was in Ukraine right after Lindsey announced this legislation — and I've been working with him for a year on this — that "now is the time." There was excitement in the air. The EU commissioner supports this bill. Our allies support this bill.

We are free to have disagreements — that’s democracy. But when we’re addressing our adversaries, we need to speak as one — with one voice, as one nation. They need to know that we’re not divided when it comes to our national security.

The senate passed this bill 86-11 for God's sake. That is an overwhelming bipartisan support. Now, it’s time for the House to unite and do the same.

Think about this. If this bill fails, the message that that would send to our adversaries — Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea — all of whom want to see this bill go down today, would be celebrated in the streets.

Make no mistake: Putin is watching. President Xi is watching. The Ayatollah is watching. Kim Jong Un is watching. If the United States Congress can’t rally around such broadly supported legislation, what message would that send to them?

This is a critical national security issue — but it also is a moral issue that requires moral courage.

When we look back on this moment in time, I want us to be able to say that we used all the tools available to end this war. That we understood the threat. That we had the courage to do what was right — to cripple the Russian war machine and turn the tide toward peace. To be on the right side of history.

In his final press conference, Senator Graham said, quote, “I have never been more optimistic than I am today that we have the formula to end this war.” This is the formula — this bill. I couldn’t agree more with the late Lindsey Graham, my friend and mentor.

Let me be clear, in closing: A vote for this bill is a vote for Ukraine and the free world. A vote against this bill is a vote for Putin and his unholy alliance.

I urge my colleagues on both sides of the aisle [to vote yes]. You don't have many votes like this in the Congress that impact global, geopolitical conflicts. This bill will have a direct impact on the conflict threatening Eastern Europe and NATO itself and can bring this to an end to get Putin to the negotiating table.

For as now, as Zelensky told me, he's ready for a ceasefire. He's ready to negotiate. It's Mr. Putin that will not call for a ceasefire. He will not negotiate.

This bill will bring him to the table, and that's why, Mr. Speaker, it is so important at this time in history.

title: Chairwoman McClain Secures $50 Million for Water Projects in House-Passed WRDA bill
text:
WASHINGTON – House Republican Conference Chairwoman Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) today secured authorization for $50,000,000 in water infrastructure projects in Lapeer, Macomb, Oakland, and St. Clair Counties in the Water Resources Development Act (WRDA) of 2026. The legislation now heads to the Senate for further consideration.

“When you turn on the tap, you expect clean, safe drinking water to come out,” Chairwoman McClain said. “But as many families in Michigan know, aging infrastructure means we can’t take that for granted. This $50 million authorization will help communities upgrade the water systems families and businesses rely on every single day.

The legislation comes after a May 2026 water main break left families and businesses in Lake Orion and surrounding communities without running water for days. Subject to appropriations, the funding authorized by WRDA 2026will allow the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to partner with local communities to improve water supply resiliency in the future.

title: McClellan Statement on Sanctions Against Russia and Granting Trump Unilateral Tariff Authority
text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, Congresswoman Jennifer McClellan (VA-04) issued the following statement after the House voted to pass H.R. 5334, the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026:

“At a time when the cost of everything from gas to groceries, health care to housing, technology to toilet paper and more keeps going up, the Trump Administration keeps doubling down on the cost-of-living crisis through needless tariffs on allies and adversaries alike with no discretion. Though I support implementing sanctions against Russia, I cannot support a sanctions bill that grants the Trump Administration greater tariff authority to prolong and intensify ongoing economic uncertainty.

“Russia’s illegal war against Ukraine demands a serious response, and I stand firmly on the side of the Ukrainian people and their struggle against Putin’s invasion of their country. The U.S. must continue its role of providing support for Ukraine while holding Russia accountable. Unfortunately, rather than solely working to strengthen and enact tougher sanctions on Russia and deliver military aid to Ukraine, this bill also contains the largest transfer of tariff authority ever granted to a president by Congress, allowing the Trump Administration to launch 100% tariffs on any country it chooses without Congressional guardrails. And Trump, just off the heels of starting an unnecessary trade war with Canada, has given every indication that he would exploit this power to entrench the American people in more trade wars, which would only further drive up costs.

“In a government that hinges on checks and balances, we cannot further cede Congress’s constitutional authority to levy tariffs and allow the executive to operate with total tariff power. To address Russia’s war in Ukraine, we need substantive action that both sanctions Russia and its allies for their aggression and equips Ukraine with the tools necessary to defend itself and push back against Putin’s war machine. This is not that legislation. For that reason, I voted no.”

title: Congresswoman McCollum Votes Against Expanded Presidential Tariff Powers
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C.— Today, the House of Representatives voted on The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act. Congresswoman McCollum voted against the legislation that would hand expanded tariff powers to President Trump. Following the vote, Congresswoman McCollum released the following statement:

“This bill is a wolf in sheep’s clothing. While purporting to be a bill to sanction Russia, this bill is so broad that it passes tariff authority into law that could hit the majority of our trading partners. I refuse to give expanded tariff authority to a president that routinely wages reckless trade wars with our closest allies.

“The U.S. must implement enforceable sanctions against Russia to bring an end to their illegal and devasting war against Ukraine. This bill fails to mandate those penalties for Russia’s aggression. Instead, this legislation only directs the president to put sanctions on Russia if he chooses. I want sanctions on Russia, period, and President Trump already has the power to do so without this bill.

“For a president who says he supports Ukraine, he has inexplicably delayed release the $400 million dollars that Congress appropriated last spring to support Ukraine. President Trump must immediately release these funds that are so desperately needed to defend Ukraine from Russia’s aggression.”

title: Congressman McCormick Chairs Critical Hearing on Biotechnology Amid Race with China for Global Leadership
text:
Washington, D.C. — Today, Congressman Rich McCormick (GA-07), Chairman of the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee’s Subcommittee on Investigations and Oversight, chaired a hearing examining America’s biotechnology leadership, federal oversight of high-risk biological research, and the growing biotechnology race with the Chinese Communist Party.

The Subcommittee heard testimony from Dr. Anemone Franz, Visiting Research Fellow at the American Enterprise Institute; Mr. Joshua Hodges, Visiting Fellow at the Hoover Institution; and Dr. Gigi Gronvall, Professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

“American biotechnology has long been one of our nation’s greatest strategic assets, but that leadership is no longer guaranteed,” said Congressman McCormick. “The Chinese Communist Party has made biotechnology a national priority, just as it has with semiconductors and artificial intelligence. We cannot afford to be complacent. We must protect American research, strengthen oversight, and ensure the breakthroughs funded by American taxpayers translate into American jobs, American manufacturing, and American strength.”

The hearing examined federal oversight of high-risk biological research, including gain-of-function research, as well as the growing convergence of artificial intelligence and biotechnology. McCormick emphasized both the enormous potential of AI to accelerate drug discovery, protein design, and biomanufacturing and the need to prevent American research, data, and technology from being exploited by adversaries.

McCormick has also introduced two bills to strengthen American biotechnology leadership. The Biotechnology Workforce Alignment Act (H.R. 8398) would better align federal biotechnology research investments with the skilled workforce needed to develop and scale those innovations here at home. The Biotechnology Diplomacy Leadership Act (H.R. 9755) would strengthen U.S. leadership abroad by coordinating American biotechnology policy and confronting threats from adversaries seeking access to American data, technology, and capabilities.

title: Reps. McDonald Rivet, Davis Lead New Push to Stop Tax Giveaways for Data Centers
text:
*WATCH REP. McDONALD RIVET’S OPENING REMARKS HERE*

WASHINGTON— Today, Representatives Kristen McDonald Rivet (MI-08) and Don Davis (NC-01) led 25 Members of Congress in introducing the Reverse Big Ugly Tax Breaks for Data Centers Act, which would rein in tax giveaways for data center development.

Last year, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) significantly expanded tax breaks that have helped spur the construction of AI data centers; that same legislation cut over $1 trillion from Medicaid and SNAP food assistance. The Reverse Big Ugly Tax Breaks for Data Centers Act would exclude data centers from benefiting from those OBBBA tax breaks. Specifically, the bill would exclude data centers from being able to take the 100% bonus depreciation tax deduction, and from being eligible for Opportunity Zone tax benefits.

Congresswoman McDonald Rivet said, “Washington is giving handouts to Big Tech companies while American families are drowning — I hear that word, ‘drowning,’ all the time from working parents back home. Tax cuts need to go to families, not data centers. We absolutely should not cut health care and food assistance for children and seniors to pay for tax giveaways to corporations. We have to fix it.”

Congressman Davis said, “When families are struggling at the pump, in the grocery store, and with rising utility bills, we cannot give data centers a blank check. We need time to fully understand the costs and consequences of these projects, including their impact on power grids, water systems, and utility costs for rural communities across eastern North Carolina and our nation.”

The bill text can be found HERE, and a one-pager on the bill can be found HERE.

Other members introducing the bill include Representatives Kathy Castor (FL-14), Sharice Davids (KS-03), Madeleine Dean (PA-04), Chris Deluzio (PA-17), Vicente Gonzalez (TX-34), Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07), Greg Landsman (OH-01), Rick Larsen (WA-02), Mike Levin (CA-49), John Mannion (NY-22), April McClain Delaney (MD-06), Betty McCollum (MN-04), Jimmy Panetta (CA-19), Chris Pappas (NH-01), Deborah Ross (NC-02), Andrea Salinas (OR-06), Greg Stanton (AZ-04), Dina Titus (NV-01), Norma Torres (CA-35), Derek Tran (CA-45), Gabe Vasquez (NM-02), Eugene Vindman (VA-07), and Debbie Wasserman Schultz (FL-25).

title: Rep. John McGuire Celebrates Passage of Bill to Shield Residents from Data Center Costs
text:
September 16, 2026

WASHINGTON, D.C. — On Wednesday, Representative John McGuire (VA-05) celebrated the passage of the Ratepayer Protection Act, which will protect Americans from carrying the financial burden of data centers in their communities.

“Data centers are necessary, but each individual community should have the right to decide where they are located," said Rep. John McGuire (VA-05). "They should not negatively affect water tables or pass their energy costs on to ratepayers. The Ratepayer Protection Act ensures we can remain strong in the AI race against China while protecting hard-working Americans from financial burdens. We will continue to find ways to invest in American infrastructure while keeping costs low for the people who make our nation strong.”

Background:

The bill requires state utility regulators and nonregulated utilities to consider implementing a standard to hold certain large-load customers responsible for the costs associated with any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade of electric service necessary to serve such customers.

A large-load customer means a non-residential electric consumer that enters, or requests to enter, an agreement concerning the sale of electric energy primarily to operate information technology infrastructure and related systems pertaining to data storage and computational applications and services (e.g., data centers) that have a peak electric demand of 100 megawatts or more at a single site or campus.

This rate must include the costs that would be incurred if the large-load customer terminates an agreement with the electric utility pertaining to the sale of electric energy or otherwise ceases the purchase of energy from the electric utility.

title: House Small Business Committee Advances Mejia Bill to Ensure Accurate Disaster Assistance Information
text:
For Immediate Release: September 16, 2026

Contact: Beth Wiesinger | NJ11AMPress@Mail.House.Gov

Disaster Loan Outreach Consistency Act would require SBA to provide consistent, current disaster loan information to small business owners

WASHINGTON, D.C. — The House Committee on Small Business today advanced legislation introduced by Representative Analilia Mejia (NJ-11) to strengthen federal disaster assistance for small businesses and ensure owners have accurate, up-to-date information when recovering from natural disasters. The legislation will advance to the House floor when scheduled for a vote.

Small businesses are increasingly on the front lines of natural disasters, facing flooding, severe storms, blizzards, and other events that can threaten their ability to stay open. The Disaster Loan Outreach Consistency Act would require the Small Business Administration (SBA) to establish standardized procedures to ensure disaster outreach materials are consistent, current, and accurate across its field operations centers—equipping businesses with the information to seek and receive aid in a timely manner.

“With nearly 99 percent of all businesses in my home state of New Jersey are small businesses and each one facing the threat of coastal storms and severe floods, these are over 1 million owners and potential borrowers who need all the relevant information. This is why my bill, the Disaster Loan Outreach Consistency Act, offers a simple solution and basic oversight to this issue,” said Congresswoman Mejia. “I urge my colleagues and members of this committee to support this legislation. In a period of time where misinformation is rampant, we must work to ensure small business owners have all the possible information they can have to make the best decision for themselves. We cannot let our federal agencies misguide, misdirect, and withhold vital information, especially when they make regulatory changes that affect Americans. The disaster loan program is one crucial step in recovery after a natural disaster.”

Small businesses make up nearly 99 percent of businesses in New Jersey, making access to reliable disaster assistance particularly important as communities across the state face increasingly severe storms and flooding.

The legislation would provide greater consistency and accountability across SBA’s disaster outreach efforts, helping ensure that the small business owners who rely on federal disaster loans receive the information they need to make informed decisions and recover more quickly.

title: Menendez Legislation to Strengthen Electric Grid Planning Amid Rapidly Growing Energy Demand Passes the House
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Last night, Congressman Rob Menendez (NJ-08) announced that his bipartisan legislation, the Load Forecasting Enhancement Act, passed the House of Representatives. The legislation, introduced in June with Congressman Troy Balderson (OH-12), would help protect families and strengthen grid planning amid rapidly growing energy demand due to AI data centers.

“Families across America are facing rapidly rising utility bills as a result of unprecedented strain on our power grids, including increased demand from AI data centers,” said Congressman Menendez. “I am pleased that our legislation has passed the House of Representatives and is one step closer to becoming law. We will continue working to lower energy costs for families, protect ratepayers, and ensure our electrical grid can meet growing needs.”

“To protect Americans from higher electric bills and make sure our grid can keep up with rising demand, we need to plan ahead,” said Congressman Balderson. “The bipartisan Load Forecasting Enhancement Act gives states and utilities the tools they need to better understand future electricity demand and prepare for it. I applaud my House colleagues for supporting this practical legislation and helping make electricity reliable and more affordable for American families.”

The bill directs the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) to convene regional joint boards with state public utility commissions to identify best practices for electric load forecasting. The legislation also requires FERC to report its findings and recommendations to Congress and encourages states to consider adopting improved forecasting procedures to support reliable, affordable electric service.

The United States is experiencing unprecedented growth in electricity usage and demand. At the same time, the North American Electric Reliability Corporation’s 2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment warns that much of North America faces a growing risk of energy shortfalls over the next five years, with PJM—the regional transmission organization serving New Jersey—classified as “high risk.” Accurate load forecasting is critical to ensuring that the electric grid can meet future demand without blackouts or forcing consumers to pay for unnecessary infrastructure.

In addition to directing FERC to develop recommendations for improving load forecasting, the legislation:

Amends the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act to encourage state consideration of those recommendations; and

Updates the Policy and Conservation Act to promote greater accuracy, oversight, and transparency in utility forecasting practices.

Congressman Menendez serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where he has been a leader on tackling rising costs for families in New Jersey and across the country. He recently introduced legislation to address skyrocketing energy bills and the environmental impacts of AI data centers across the country. To learn more about his work, click here.

title: MENG INTRODUCES THE STAMPS FOR STAYING CONNECTED ACT
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Congresswoman Grace Meng (D-NY) introduced the Stamps for Staying Connected Act (H.R.10129), a bill that provides postage to incarcerated individuals who cannot afford it.

This legislation would authorize the Director of the Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP) to provide postage for general correspondence to incarcerated individuals who lack sufficient funds in their commissary accounts. While the BOP already provides postage for legal-related mail, this measure would codify that policy and extend it to personal correspondence by providing up to five stamps per week for general mail, in addition to the five stamps currently available for legal-related mail.

Federal prisons currently require individuals to use funds from their commissary accounts to purchase postage. But many incarcerated people have little or no money available. Federal prison jobs can pay as little as 12 cents per hour, meaning it can take several hours of work to earn enough to purchase a single stamp.

“People who are incarcerated rely on mail to stay connected with their families and loved ones, prepare for reentry, pursue education, practice their faith, and communicate with their attorneys,” said Congresswoman Meng. “Providing a few stamps each week is a basic but meaningful way to help people maintain those critical connections while they are serving their time. This commonsense legislation builds on an existing BOP policy so that people in prison do not have to spend the little money they earn each day simply to write home.”

Staying connected with family, friends, faith communities, and other support networks can help people successfully return to their communities after incarceration. The Bureau of Prisons encourages people in its custody to maintain these relationships, and research shows that strong support systems can reduce recidivism and improve reentry outcomes after release

"Maintaining family and community connections is one of the strongest predictors of successful reentry and safer communities,” said Nina Patel, Senior Policy Counsel, Justice Division, American Civil Liberties Union. “However, many people in federal prison cannot afford the cost of a postage stamp. The Stamps for Staying Connected Act recognizes that meaningful rehabilitation depends on preserving relationships for people who are incarcerated. Sending a letter home can strengthen a parent's bond with a child, sustain hope, and reinforce the support systems that help people return to their communities successfully. This commonsense legislation will help ensure people in federal prison are not cut off from the very connections that provide meaning and support for rehabilitation."

“When incarcerated people are able to stay connected to their families, it helps boost their mental health and can ease their transition back home after they’re released,” said JC Hendrickson, senior policy strategist in the Brennan Center's Justice Program. “But many people incarcerated in federal prison cannot afford stamps, making it difficult to send letters to loved ones. This bill would help make sure that everyone behind bars can communicate with their families.”

“Communicating with family members in prison should not depend on how much money someone has,” said Shanna Rifkin, FAMM General Counsel. “This bill would help people in prison foster relationships with loved ones that we know are crucial for improved mental health and also reduced recidivism once people return to the community.”

“NYC Books Through Bars, a prison literacy project, sends free books in response to letters we receive from people who are incarcerated in facilities around the country,” said Daniel Schaffer, NYC Books Through Bars. “We know that the stamps needed to write to us are a precious resource, and we are likely failing to serve the neediest population—those with nothing in their commissary. If people in federal prisons were regularly provided stamps, they would not have to choose between staying in touch with their families, seeking legal advice from their lawyers, and writing to us to request books that are critical to their survival behind bars.”

“For many incarcerated people, the cost of postage is a barrier to staying connected with their loved ones,” said Aleks Kajstura, Sr. Policy & Advocacy Analyst, Prison Policy Initiative. “Improving family contact is critical for the health and reentry outcomes of people in prison. Requiring that the Bureau of Prisons provide stamps to people who cannot afford the cost of sending a letter makes it easier for everyone to achieve those goals.”

The bill is cosponsored by Reps. Yvette Clarke, Sydney Kamlager-Dove, Eleanor Norton-Holmes, and Nydia Velazquez. It is supported by American Civil Liberties Union, Brennan Center for Justice, Citizens Against Recidivism, Families Against Mandatory Minimums (FAMM), Fortune Society, Justice Action Network, NYC Books Through Bars, Prison Policy Initiative, and Social Workers and Allies Against Solitary Confinement.

title: Rep. Kennedy passes eighth bill, more than any Utah first term Congressman in history

title: THOMPSON JOINS 106 LAWMAKERS IN CALLING ON SPEAKER JOHNSON TO PASS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE SAFEGUARDS
text:
Washington – Rep. Mike Thompson (CA-04) joined 106 colleagues in calling on Speaker Johnson to reconvene the House of Representatives to address the risks posed by advanced artificial intelligence (AI). A series of whistleblowers working in the AI industry have raised concerns in recent weeks that without new guardrails, rapidly developing AI technology could cause job losses, mass cybersecurity breaches, the development of biological or chemical weapons, and other threats. Some experts have even warned that superintelligent AI could defy human instructions.

Public disclosures from the companies and researchers developing the world’s most capable AI systems underscore the need to act. In July, over 1,300 top employees of the leading AI companies called on the U.S. government to act by supporting an international effort to develop tools that can slow down AI development. Since then, a series of proposals have emerged from members of Congress on both sides of the aisle that would provide the transparency and evaluation that is desperately needed. Despite this, Speaker Johnson and House Republican leadership have yet to bring any of these proposals to the floor for a vote and intend to send lawmakers home for a 6-week break at the end of this week.

"Reasonable minds may disagree about precisely how Congress should regulate this rapidly evolving technology. We cannot disagree about the imperative for Congress to act," wrote the lawmakers. "AI experts and leading companies agree that the United States can lead the world in artificial intelligence while establishing reasonable safeguards that protect Americans and our national security. We can—and must—do both."

"The House should return to Washington immediately and remain in session until Congress advances meaningful, bipartisan AI safeguards.” continued the lawmakers.

The full text of the letter can be found HERE and below.

The Honorable Mike Johnson Speaker

U.S. House of Representatives

H-232, The Capitol Washington D.C. 20515

Dear Speaker Johnson: We write to urge you to immediately reconvene the House of Representatives to enable Congress to take urgent action to address catastrophic risk posed by advanced artificial intelligence. Those risks take any of several forms, separately and in combination—of agentic misalignment, mass cybersecurity breaches, and development of biological or chemical weapons.

Reasonable minds may disagree about precisely how Congress should regulate this rapidly evolving technology. We cannot disagree about the imperative for Congress to act.

Instead of action, you have announced vacation. After a month-long August recess, the House leadership changed the schedule to announce two more weeks of vacation–immediately prior to yet another month of recess in October.

Ample evidence—in the form of a series of public disclosures from the companies and researchers developing the world's most capable AI systems—underscore the urgency of the moment:

In July, OpenAI models undergoing cybersecurity evaluations bred swarms of agents that circumvented controls designed to isolate them from the internet, conspired to exploit vulnerabilities, hacked third party systems, and alter evidence of their activity, an incident that OpenAI has called a "warning shot," about the risks of highly capable rogue AI agents.

Days later, more than 1,300 top employees of frontier AI companies called on the U.S. government to support an international effort to develop tools that can “deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.”

More recently, Anthropic disrupted cases in which researchers used Claude for biological research that could have aided the development of biological weapons, and called biological misuse “one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models.”

Anthropic also documented China-linked actors using Claude for surveillance and transnational repression, and Iran-linked actors using it for propaganda, mass surveillance, and targeting recommendations against U.S. naval forces.

Meanwhile, CISA reported Chinese open-weight models accelerating their capabilities through “industrial-scale” distillation of American models—giving rise to AI agents nearly as powerful as the top U.S. frontier models, yet wholly unconstrained by American authorities or by U.S. safeguards.

These disclosures must not constitute yet another in a long series of “warning shots,” but rather, a starting gun. Congress must act. A series of proposals have emerged from our colleagues that deserve consideration, public debate, thoughtful amendment, and action. They include bills mandating transparency and evaluation of frontier models, “kill switch” requirements, and a waiver of antitrust laws to enable critical industry-wide collaboration on safety and security. Whether with these proposals or any other variants, AI experts and leading companies agree that the United States can lead the world in artificial intelligence while establishing reasonable safeguards that protect Americans and our national security. We can—and must—do both.

While AI safety experts and Americans increasingly urge action to confront this conflagration of risk, Congress fiddles. When we did return to work after the August recess, we consumed floor time with debates and votes on performative resolutions opposing socialism. After next week, the House resumes its vacation—for another six weeks.

You can forgive every American who believes that Congress remains unserious about confronting our nation’s most pressing challenges.

The House should return to Washington immediately and remain in session until Congress advances meaningful, bipartisan AI safeguards. To our children who will have read a post-apocalyptic history, “Why Congress Slept” —likely written by agentic AI—our inaction will be inexplicable, and unforgivable.

Sincerely

###

Congressman Mike Thompson is proud to represent California’s 4th Congressional District, which includes all or part of Lake, Napa, Solano, Sonoma and Yolo Counties. He is a senior member of the House Committee on Ways and Means. Rep. Thompson is Chairman of the House Gun Violence Prevention Task Force. He is also Co-Chair of the bipartisan, bicameral Congressional Wine Caucus and a member of the fiscally-responsible Blue Dog Coalition.

title: Miller-Meeks, Ernst Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act Passes Congress, Heads to President’s Desk
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. House of Representatives has given final passage to the bipartisan Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act, legislation led by Congresswoman Mariannette Miller-Meeks (IA-01) and U.S. Senator Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) requiring public disclosure of taxpayer-funded projects that are more than $1 billion over budget or more than five years behind schedule.

The House originally passed H.R. 1722, the Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act, in July 2026. Both Chambers have now given final approval, sending the bill to President Trump’s desk.

“Iowans work hard for their money, and they expect Washington to be a good steward of every taxpayer dollar,” said Congresswoman Miller-Meeks. “When billion-dollar projects go years over schedule and billions over budget, taxpayers deserve answers and accountability. The Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act will shine a light on these financial train wrecks and make sure Congress and the American people know where their money is going. I’m proud to see this bill pass Congress and head to the President’s desk, and I thank Senator Ernst for her partnership in getting this important legislation across the finish line.”

“Going a billion dollars over budget isn’t a rounding error—it’s a financial trainwreck at taxpayers’ expense,” said Sen. Ernst. “Taxpayers deserve transparency, and this legislation will shine a light on these boondoggles and hold Washington accountable for its out-of-control spending.”

"Congress must ensure that every taxpayer dollar is spent efficiently. Every year, there are government projects that are above cost projections or behind schedule. Congress has a duty to root out government waste and mismanagement to protect the American taxpayer. The Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act brings transparency to failing government projects to prevent waste of Americans’ tax dollars. I thank Congresswoman Miller-Meeks for championing this legislation," said House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform Chairman James Comer (R-Ky.).

Background:

The legislation follows a report from Senator Ernst exposingmore than a dozen government projects that collectively racked up $162 billion in cost overruns. Meanwhile, the national debt has surpassed$40 trillion, growing by over $2 trillion in the past year alone, and the Government Accountability Office has documented$2.7 trillion in improper payments by federal agencies since 2003.

Some of the worst boondoggles this bill would expose:

California High-Speed Rail — more than $150 billion over budget, from an original $33 billion estimate to as much as $231 billion.

VA electronic health record system — tripled from $16.1 billion to $49.8 billion, with flaws that may have contributed to veteran deaths.

Honolulu Rail Transit — $4.8 billion over budget, with completion slipping from 2020 to 2031.

Washington Metro's Purple Line — $3.1 billion over budget and more than five years delayed.

Columbus Crossroads corridor — 19 years behind schedule, with costs more than double the original $801 million estimate.

Air Force One replacements — billions over budget and years behind schedule.

Federal Reserve renovation — up 34% from $1.9 billion to nearly $2.5 billion.

Congresswoman Miller-Meeks has been a leading voice in the fight against government waste, fraud, and abuse. She first introduced the Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act in the 118th Congress and reintroduced it in the 119th Congress alongside Senator Ernst.

title: Rep. Min Leads OC Delegation in Bipartisan Bill to Name Irvine Post Office After Songbird of Manzanar, Mary Kageyama Nomura
text:
Washington, DC. — Representative Dave Min (CA-47) introduced legislation to designate the United States Postal Service facility located in Irvine as the “Mary Kageyama Nomura Post Office Building,” honoring the life and legacy of Mary Kageyama Nomura, widely known as the “Songbird of Manzanar.”

If enacted, the legislation would make the Irvine facility the first United States post office named in honor of a Japanese American who was incarcerated during World War II at a concentration camp.

“Mary Kageyama Nomura lived through one of the darkest chapters in our nation’s history, but she never allowed that injustice to extinguish her hope or her commitment to others,” said Rep. Min. “At Manzanar, her music brought comfort and joy to a community that had been stripped of its freedom and dignity simply because of its ancestry. Naming this Irvine post office in her honor is a small but meaningful way to preserve her extraordinary legacy of resilience, hope, and community for generations to come.”

Born in Los Angeles in 1925, Nomura was a teenager when the United States entered World War II. After losing both of their parents within four years, Nomura and her siblings were living on their own in Venice, California, when the federal government forcibly incarcerated them at the Manzanar War Relocation Center along with thousands of other Japanese Americans. While incarcerated, Nomura became known for her remarkable singing voice. Her performances offered moments of joy and comfort amid the hardship of camp life, earning her the enduring nickname “Songbird of Manzanar.”

Following the war, Nomura and her husband built a life in Orange County, opening Shi’s Fish Mart in Garden Grove. She remained deeply involved in the Southern California Japanese American community and continued singing and participating in Manzanar reunions throughout her life. Nomura passed away earlier this year at the age of 100.

Min’s legislation is supported by Reps. Mike Thompson (D-CA-04), Jill Tokuda (D-HI-02), Maxine Waters (D-CA-43), Brad Sherman (D-CA-32), Mark Takano (D-CA-39), Judy Chu (D-CA-28), Mike Levin (D-CA-49), Zoe Lofgren (D-CA-18), Linda Sánchez (D-CA-38), Derek Tran (D-CA-45), Darrell Issa (R-CA-48), Celeste Maloy (R-UT-02), James Gallagher (R-CA-01), Kimberlyn King-Hinds (R-MP-At Large), Aumua Amata Coleman Radewagen (R-AS-At Large), Brad Finstad (R-MN-01), Young Kim (R-CA-40), Ken Calvert (R-CA-41), and Kevin Kiley (I-CA-03).

title: Griffith Votes to Protect Ninth District Communities from Footing Bill for Data Centers
text:
Today, the U.S. House of Representatives passed H.R. 9340 – the Ratepayer Protection Act. This legislation protects local communities from electricity cost hikes by directing state regulators to make data center companies pay the full cost for its use of electricity infrastructure. Under the bill, all state utility commissions will hold proceedings on large-load electric rates and rules for data centers that draw more than 100 MW of power. The bill now heads to the U.S. Senate for further consideration.

Following House passage of the bill, U.S. Congressman Morgan Griffith (R-VA), who voted for the bill and is a co-sponsor of similar legislation, issued the following statement:

“With this bill, data centers are on notice. Under the watch of this Congress, I will continue to promote responsible federal guardrails while supporting local autonomy over data centers.”

Congressman Griffith is also a co-sponsor of H.R. 6529 – the Protecting Families from AI Data Center Energy Costs Act.

title: Moylan, Terrirotires & Commonwealths Caucus Press Administration for De Minimis Relief
text:
(Washington D.C.) — Congressman Moylan, along with fellow members of the Congressional Territories & Commonwealths Caucus, sent a letter to key federal officials pressing for a meeting with the Administration to address recent de minimis changes affecting residents and businesses across the U.S. territories.

Moylan was joined by Resident Commissioner Pablo José Hernández (D-Puerto Rico), Congresswoman Aumua Amata Coleman Radewagen (R-American Samoa), Congresswoman Stacey Plaskett (D-U.S. Virgin Islands), and Congresswoman Kimberlyn King-Hinds (R-CNMI).

Together, the members requested a meeting with representatives from the White House, Department of the Treasury, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, and U.S. Postal Service to discuss recent duty collection requirements affecting mail originating from the territories and work toward a resolution for their constituents.

The Caucus raised concerns over the elimination of the $800 de minimis exemption and the resulting changes to customs processing requirements. While the suspension of duty-free de minimis treatment was intended to address broader trade concerns, the members said its application is now affecting individuals and businesses in U.S. territories outside of the U.S. customs territory.

“This is affecting people across the territories, not just Guam,” said Congressman Moylan. “That is why we are raising this issue together. Our residents and businesses already deal with higher shipping costs and fewer options. We should be looking for ways to make things easier for them, not adding another hurdle. We want to sit down with the Administration, work through these concerns, and find a solution that recognizes the realities our communities face.”

The members noted that Guam, the CNMI, American Samoa, and the U.S. Virgin Islands already face unique logistical and economic challenges, including higher shipping costs, geographic isolation, and limited transportation options. They expressed concern that federal trade and customs policies can place an added burden on territorial residents and businesses when those circumstances are not taken into account.

Through the requested meeting, the Caucus is seeking to better understand how the new requirements are being implemented, identify possible administrative solutions, and discuss a path toward restoring de minimis treatment for the territories.

Moylan is also backing a legislative solution. Last November, Congresswoman King-Hinds introduced H.R. 5960, the Territorial De Minimis Exemption Act, alongside Moylan, Congresswoman Radewagen, and Congresswoman Plaskett. The legislation would permanently provide a de minimis exemption for U.S. territories outside of the U.S. customs territory.
