title: Congressman Vicente Gonzalez Introduces Bill to Federally Recognize Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas
text:
Contact: Alexis Torres

Washington, D.C. – Ahead of the Lipan Apache Tribe’s 2026 Veterans Powwow in Corpus Christi, Texas, on Saturday, September 19th, Congressman Vicente Gonzalez (TX-34) introduced H.R. 10435, the Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas Recognition Act. This legislation would grant the Tribe and its members access to all of the rights, services and benefits provided by the Federal Government to federally recognized Indian Tribes.

“The Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas has made significant cultural and historical contributions to the United States. From serving in our military and protecting the environment and sacred sites to much more, they are our trusted neighbors—deeply woven into the fabric of South Texas. It is long overdue for Congress to officially recognize this Tribe and expand their access to federal support and resources,” said Congressman Gonzalez.

"Introduction of this legislation marks a historic step forward for the Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas. For centuries, our people have maintained our community, culture, and identity, with our ancestors having relationships with Spain, Mexico, the Republic of Texas, and the United States. We are grateful to Congressman Vicente Gonzalez for his leadership. Today brings us one important step closer to the federal recognition our people have long deserved," said Bernard F. Barcena, Jr., Chairman of The Lipan Apache Tribe.

"For generations, the Lipan Apache people have fought to preserve our faith, ceremonies, and sacred traditions. I know personally what it means to have to fight for the freedom to practice our religion simply because our Tribe lacks federal recognition. While that fight secured important protections for some of our people, religious freedom should not depend on a court case. This legislation is an important step toward ensuring that all enrolled members of the tribe can practice our faith and preserve our sacred traditions with the dignity and freedom they deserve," said Dr. Robert Soto, Vice-Chairman of The Lipan Apache Tribe.

The Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas is the successor to historic Lipan Apache bands that maintained an independent Tribal identity and political organization within present-day Texas for centuries before and after Spanish, Mexican, Republic of Texas, and United States sovereignty.

When Texas became a U.S. state in 1845, the Lipan Apache faced immense hardship from the impacts of smallpox, war, and attacks by other American Indians and non-Indians. The Tribe, which once lived in parts of Texas, New Mexico, and Mexico, was displaced to areas of South Texas, including the Rio Grande Valley, Coastal Bend, and the Big Bend region of West Texas.

Notably, the Texas Legislature honored the Lipan Apache Tribe through legislative resolutions in 2009. In 2014, a federal court ordered the U.S. Department of Interior to return confiscated eagle feathers to Tribal Vice-Chairman Dr. Robert Soto and other plaintiffs. The decision subsequently allowed certain Tribal member plaintiffs to possess and obtain eagle feathers and feathers of other protected migratory birds—noting that no one was contesting the fact that the plaintiffs were American Indians. Due to the lack of formal federal recognition, most tribal members do not have the right currently, which makes practicing tribal ceremonies and personal religions difficult. The Texas Legislature and Governor reconfirmed the significant contributions of the Tribe to our state through resolutions in 2019. In 2021, the City and County of Presidio transferred the deed to El Cementerio de los Lipanes en el Barrio de los Lipanes, a sacred site for the Lipan Apache Tribe.

The Federal Government, including the Department of Interior Indian Affairs, and many other agencies, serves federally recognized tribes through its government-to-government relationships to support the development of tribal governments, strong economies, and quality programs spanning from education, social services, law enforcement, resource protection, and more.

title: Goodlander, Escobar Express Concern for Apparent Lack of Support for VA Advisory Committee on Women Veterans
text:
Washington, D.C. – This week, Representatives Maggie Goodlander (NH-2) and Veronica Escobar (TX-16) led a group of ten Democratic Members of Congress in a letter to Secretary of Veterans Affairs (VA) Doug Collins expressing their concern for the apparent lack of support for the VA Advisory Committee on Women Veterans (ACWV).

The full letter can be found here and below:

Secretary Collins:

We write to express our concern regarding the apparent lack of support for the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Advisory Committee on Women Veterans (ACWV). According to the ACWV Charter, which you signed October 6, 2025, this Federal Advisory Committee (FAC) must meet twice annually and submit a report to the Secretary of Veterans Affairs annually on July 1st. However, according to the files assembled and maintained by VA’s Advisory Committee Management Office in accordance with the law, the committee has not met since December 2024. No report has been published for either 2025 or 2026.

Additionally, we understand that the most recent Chair of the ACWV, Colonel (Ret.) Wanda A. Wright, resigned from that position in April 2026 in protest of VA having “effectively rendered the Committee inactive” and affirming the digital record of inactivity referenced above by noting the ACWV has not met since December 2024.

Under the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA), it is a requirement that advisory committees meet regularly, conduct business transparently, and actively fulfill their statutory purpose. Specifically, the ACWV is mandated by statute, 38 U.S.C. § 542, which requires that the Secretary of Veterans Affairs establish an advisory committee consisting of members from the general public who represent women veterans, veterans with service-connected disabilities, and those recently separated from the military and/or are recognized authorities in fields including gender-specific health-care needs of women. The law also requires you to consult with and seek advice from the ACWV with respect to VA health care, benefits, outreach, and other programs administered by VA. The committee, by statute, is to submit a report to you which you are required to submit to Congress within 60 days of receipt. We did not receive a report in 2025 and have seen no evidence that we should expect one in 2026.

The lapse in the ACWV’s required activities raises concerns about whether the Department is fulfilling its statutory obligation to consult with and seek the committee’s advice on matters affecting women veterans. The limited information available regarding the committee’s status further raises questions about whether VA is meeting its obligations under law and providing Congress and the public with adequate transparency regarding the operation of a Congressionally mandated advisory body.

To better understand the Department’s practices related to this FAC, we request responses to the following questions no later than October 2, 2026:

How many times did the VA Advisory Committee on Women Veterans meet in 2025?

As of the date of your response, how many times has the ACWV met in 2026?

What is informing your decisions about how to optimally provide care, benefits, and

services to women veterans in the absence of regular meetings of the ACWV?

Each FAC has an associated budget and employees. Given that ACWV has not met as

required in 2025 and 2026, have the budget and employees been redirected and if so how are they being used? Please provide funding levels used to support FAC activities in

FY2025 and FY2026 and descriptions of how the funding was used.

What is your plan to ensure that meetings of the ACWV occur according to its statue and charter?

We appreciate your prompt attention to these questions and expect a timely and complete response. Congress created these advisory committees to ensure that the voices, expertise, and experiences of veterans inform the Department charged with serving them. Veterans and their families, caregivers, and survivors deserve nothing less than a clear accounting of why the Advisory Committee on Women Veterans has been allowed to fall silent and what the Department will do to restore these critical perspectives to the table.

In addition to Representatives Goodlander and Escobar, the signers of this letter include Representatives Terri Sewell (AL-7), Ed Case (HI-1), Chrissy Houlahan (PA-6), George Latimer (NY-16), Nikki Budzinski (IL-13), Tim Kennedy (NY-26), Madeleine Dean (PA-4), and Deborah Ross (NC-2).

title: RELEASE: Gottheimer Announces New Bipartisan Legislation on AI Safety to Protect Jersey Families, National Security
text:
Above: Gottheimer announces new AI safety legislation at FDU.

TEANECK, NJ — Today, Friday, September 18, 2026, U.S. Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5), Co-Chair of the House AI Commission and a senior member of the House Intelligence Committee, announced a new bipartisan agenda to put real guardrails on AI development to ensure the U.S. can win the global AI race in the right way.

Watch Gottheimer’s remarks here.

“Right now, there are no mandatory requirements for pre-deployment testing of frontier AI models,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5). “That doesn’t work in banking, it doesn’t work in food safety, it doesn’t work in medicine, and it sure as hell shouldn’t work with the technology that experts say could help build a bioweapon or take down our power grid. This isn’t about stopping AI or stifling innovation, it is about making sure — with warning signs flashing red — that we can safely deploy AI, and win the race the right way.

“Artificial intelligence is one of the most consequential technologies of our time, and we have a responsibility to make sure it strengthens our national security rather than becoming a tool for those who seek to harm Americans. The American AI Security Act takes a commonsense approach: before the most powerful AI models are deployed, we should know whether they could be used to launch devastating cyberattacks or facilitate the development of chemical, biological, or radiological weapons,” said Congressman Mike Lawler (NY-17).

Gottheimer’s AI safety agenda includes two new bipartisan pieces of federal legislation and an inquiry into the Administration’s new cybersecurity plan, including:

The American AI Security Act, co-led by Congressman Mike Lawler (NY-17), establishes a mandatory, pre-deployment national security review for the most powerful AI models. Before releasing a covered model, developers would be required to give the National Security Agency full access to evaluate whether it could be used to launch a serious cyberattack or help build a chemical, biological, or radiological weapon. The review operates on a firm clock — 30 days, with a single 30-day extension if needed — so it functions as a serious national security check rather than either a rubber stamp or endless bureaucracy. Companies would be able to provide technical support for the reviews, and appeal decisions through an expedited process modeled on the courts already used for national security cases.

The China FIREWALL Act, co-led by Congressman Nick LaLota (NY-1), keeps Chinese-developed AI off of U.S. government systems. The bill would ban all Chinese-developed open-weight AI models from government-issued devices and prohibit federal agencies from procuring software that relies on those models. The legislation builds on Gottheimer’s No DeepSeek on Government Devices Act, which became law as part of the FY26 National Defense Authorization Act and blocked the Chinese AI model DeepSeek from federal devices. The China FIREWALL Act closes the loophole that still allows other Chinese open-weight models to be used at federal agencies.

And finally, Gottheimer announced he is sending a letter to Sean Cairncross, the President’s Cyber Director, about the Administration’s new AI cybersecurity clearinghouse and how it can help the government respond to growing fears of autonomous cyberattacks.

The announcement was made at Fairleigh Dickinson University, which is launching a new state-of-the-art Health Humanics Innovation Hub, that’s designed to train the next generation of healthcare workers to use AI tools without losing the human being in front of them.

Gottheimer was joined by New Jersey State Senator Gordon Johnson, Teaneck Mayor Mark Schwartz, FDU Senior VP of Government Affairs, Robert Pignatello, Engineer Lab Director, Reggie Joseph, and students from Fairleigh Dickinson University.

Below: Gottheimer announces new AI safety legislation at FDU.

Gottheimer’s remarks as prepared for delivery.

Thank you all for having me here today, and thank you to Fairleigh Dickinson University for opening up your campus for a discussion on this critical topic.

Now, I’ve been to a lot of events at a lot of great institutions across the Fifth District, but I want to take a second to recognize FDU, because this school has a story worth telling.

It started in 1942, right down the road in Rutherford, as a little two-year junior college founded by Peter and Sally Sammartino. Today, it’s the largest private university in the entire state of New Jersey, with 12,000 students, more than 100 degree programs, and students coming here from all over the world. It’s a great American story of true leadership.

Speaking of leadership, President Avaltroni and his team have built something they call “Humanics.” The idea is simple: as AI gets built into everything, especially health care, you don’t throw out empathy, ethics, and equity.

You build them in from day one. They’re standing up a Health Humanics Innovation Hub right here on the Metropolitan Campus, which Senator Johnson helped secure funding for, that brings together a healthcare humanity lab, a storytelling data lab, and partnerships with Epic Systems to make sure the doctors and nurses of tomorrow know how to use these tools without losing sight of the human being in front of them. That’s exactly the mindset we need to bring to the AI policy debate right now – as the AI race accelerates, we have to remember that the benefits of innovation are boundless in the new opportunities they offer, but can be equally boundless in the new threats they pose.

AI can change the world. It can make our businesses more productive, help Americans develop new skills, strengthen our national security, and keep the United States at the forefront of technological innovation, especially in the competition with China. It can make incredible discoveries in medicine; it can personalize education, make government more efficient and accessible, and help workers focus more on key decisions.

But, as we learned in the last weeks with Hugging Face, and yesterday, with more disclosures from OpenAI of rogue agents with basically a mind of their own, the downsides of this transformative technology, if not controlled, are real.

In these cases, agents deceived their developers, coordinated amongst themselves, and escaped from what were supposed to be secure sandboxes. If this technology gets into the wrong hands, you can imagine the potential for destruction – cybersecurity, biosecurity, our national security. Used maliciously, the government of China or Iran or a non-state actor could wreak havoc on the world. Two weeks ago, an engineer from Anthropic quit his job, declaring that this technology “could kill us all by the end of the decade.” As Bill Gates recently put it, “AI models could begin to act against our interests, and we could lose control.”

As I just mentioned, last month, a swarm of AI agents broke out of a locked-down sandbox test, found a security hole nobody even knew existed, and used it to hack straight into Hugging Face — one of the biggest and most important AI platforms on the planet. Hundreds of AI agents were coordinating with each other on a hidden message board, running for days all on their own, and they even lied to their programmers about what they did. That incident was one of the most alarming AI-driven cybersecurity failures on record — and it was conducted without any human oversight. That might sound like a movie plot or an unreleased Terminator sequel, but unfortunately it’s not.

And that’s not the only warning sign. Two weeks ago, a researcher who worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic made headlines when he quit his job at Anthropic and posted publicly that the industry is racing toward superintelligence and, in his words, gambling with our lives. That single post got 150 million views in just a day and a half. That should tell you something about how many Americans are scared of AI’s risks, and how few of them think anyone in Washington has their back. And in response, several of the leading AI CEOs acknowledged the technology’s dangers.

The runaway agents are just one of many new challenges AI poses — there are issues related to energy, water, and data centers; deepfakes, disinformation, and discrimination; chip policy and the need to protect our children; effects on the workforce. The list goes on.

And, when you’re in a race like this one, there is a great deal of pressure to go faster, both between our leading frontier labs — including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta — and between nations, particularly our competition with the Chinese Communist Party.

Ultimately, like in the Cold War, it will decide who has the military and economic might, which countries ally with others, and who will lead the world in areas like science, health care, and the humanities. While I believe deeply that we can’t afford to lose this race, we must win in the right way, or we like during the nuclear arms race, ultimately, we will all lose. I don’t mean to sound dark, but, as a member of the Intelligence Committee and Co-Chair of the House AI Commission, I have seen the briefings.

This is not a hypothetical threat. I’ve concluded that we are at a critical crossroads … on the precipice of changes that none of us can even imagine … and either we are going to get it right, or the ramifications will be unimaginable. This is happening now, and Congress needs to act like it.

This morning, I want to focus on one area of that race that is central to how we protect our children, our families, and our national security — and that is how we test the latest AI frontier models before they are let out into the wild … before the public is able to utilize them.

Right now, there are no mandatory requirements for pre-deployment testing. We are solely reliant on the Trump Administration’s voluntary cybersecurity review process based on a June 2026 Executive Order. It’s caused mass confusion in the AI world – nobody really knows who’s covered, what the rules actually are, or what happens if you don’t play along. It seems nuts to me that we wouldn’t want to require testing from the best and brightest in our government before these models are released — to protect our cybersecurity, biosecurity, critical infrastructure — our families and our national security.

But, that’s where we are here. And why? Because there are many who believe that the AI labs can handle it themselves – or, as some of the founders suggested this past week, that they rely on third-party testers or auditors to handle it. My problem with that is multi-fold: one, there are very few of these outside testers; they have limited people, compute, and access to the labs; they lack national security clearances; they don’t have broad enough expertise on the threats posed, and they rely, in part, on the labs themselves for funding. In short, it’s like having the fox guard the hen house.

It doesn’t work in banking, it doesn’t work in food safety, it doesn’t work in medicine, and it sure as hell shouldn’t work with technology that experts say could help build a bioweapon or take down our power grid. The answer isn’t, like some have suggested, to just shut it all down. That’s not tenable. Like it or not, AI is here. We can’t just cede the race to China. If we panic or stop AI development, we won’t actually stop AI — that’s not a safeguard. China is not slowing down for anybody. We will just hand the future to Beijing. It will put us right in the bullseye of our adversary. We will just get someone else’s AI.

That brings me to what we’re actually doing about it.

First, I’m announcing the American AI Security Act — new bipartisan federal legislation that I’m introducing with Congressman Mike Lawler of New York. This bill ensures that before any company releases one of the most powerful AI models in the world, they have to give the government full access to evaluate it first — to check whether that model could be used to launch a serious cyberattack, attack our critical infrastructure, or help build a chemical, biological, or radiological weapon.

It’s a real, time-bounded review that other frontier developers can help coordinate. Not endless bureaucracy, but also not a rubber stamp. A serious national security check, with a deadline, with industry input, and a proper appeals process modeled on the courts we already use for national security cases. This isn’t about stopping AI or stifling innovation; it is about making sure — with warning signs flashing red — that we can safely deploy AI, and win the race the right way.

Second, I’m announcing the China FIREWALL Act to stop Chinese AI on all government systems.

Right now, DeepSeek is blocked on most federal devices — because I fought to put that block in place, through my No DeepSeek on Government Devices Act. It became law through last year’s defense spending bill. But, here’s the problem: other Chinese open-weight models, like Moonshot’s Kimi K3 and Alibaba’s Qwen, are still walking right through the front door of our federal agencies, and they can still buy software with these models baked in without anyone even knowing it.

So, alongside Congressman Nick LaLota of New York, I’m introducing this new bipartisan legislation to close that loophole for good — banning Chinese-developed open-weight models from government devices, and blocking agencies from procuring software that relies on them. If we can’t trust Beijing with our data, we shouldn’t allow our government to use their AI systems.

Third, I’m sending a letter to the President’s Cyber Director about the Administration’s new AI cybersecurity clearinghouse. Look, the idea behind it is the right one. But right now, it’s only built to catch known vulnerabilities. That is, the stuff we already know to look for.

It does nothing about what happens when you’ve got swarms of AI agents operating at machine speed, coordinating attacks faster than any human can respond. My letter asks the hard question: is this clearinghouse actually built for the threat we’re facing in 2026, or the threat we were facing two years ago? And it raises whether the AI supply chain itself should be treated as critical infrastructure, the same way we treat our power grid and our water systems. If AI breaks, everything built on top of it breaks with it.

This Congress alone, I’ve led more than a dozen bipartisan bills that put up immediate guardrails to keep pace with the rapid rise of AI.

There is nothing partisan about protecting our country. That’s why I’ve repeatedly teamed up with Republican and Democratic colleagues alike – and why I’m co-chairing the new AI Problem Solvers Task Force. My bills tackle critical issues from rogue AI agents and cybersecurity to commonsense consumer and child protections to AI digital literacy. These bills would both protect our families and national security, and ensure we can seize upon the opportunities ahead of us.

Unfortunately, Republican leadership has refused to directly bring any of these critical pieces of legislation to the floor for a vote. And they sent us home from Washington without acting. I think that’s a huge mistake — and, right now, every week matters for America’s safety. I strongly urge the Speaker to bring us back before the election to pass AI safety legislation like the bills I’m proposing today.

Finally, let me ask this question: How did another generation handle a technology terrifying enough to end the world, without either burying their heads in the sand or torching the relationship with their biggest rival? Go back to the Cold War.

The United States and the Soviet Union were racing each other on nuclear weapons — real enemies, real stakes, real distrust. And yet, at the height of that rivalry, President Kennedy stood up and said something that still holds up today. He said, “Among the traits the peoples of our two countries have in common, none is stronger than our mutual abhorrence of war.” Soon after, we signed a nuclear test ban treaty with the Soviets. We never stopped competing with them, but we understood that some risks are big enough that even fierce rivals have to keep the guardrails up.

That is exactly the balance we need with AI: compete like hell to win, and put real safety rails in place so winning doesn’t destroy us in the process.

Our country has never been a country that waits around scared of the future — we go out, and we build it, safely, and better than anyone else on Earth. The choice is not between innovation and responsibility. We need both. We need Americans to know that as AI becomes more powerful, there are commonsense guardrails in place.

I believe that if we keep working together across the aisle for our future, in the greatest country in the world, our best days will always be ahead of us.

Thank you, God bless you, and God bless the United States of America.

title: Rep. Grijalva Raises Alarm on Deteriorating Conditions at Eloy Detention Center
text:
Detainees have reported no access to drinking water, edible food, or AC

Washington, D.C. — Congresswoman Adelita S. Grijalva took to the House floor to sound the alarm about deteriorating conditions at the Eloy Detention Center in Arizona, following multiple reports her office has received from family members of detainees and their lawyers. They report detainees receiving only “ice chips” instead of proper drinking water, inedible food, and several housing units without air conditioning.

Rep. Grijalva has completed five oversight visits of immigration detention facilities since taking office, including her first oversight visit as a Congresswoman to the facility in Eloy, which ultimately led to the release of Julia “La abuela” Benitez, a 79 year-old Cuban asylum seeker with dementia who was held there for nine months. In July, 120 detainees signed a letter outlining human rights abuses by the guards at the Eloy facility, which is privately operated by Core Civic.

Watch the full speech here. A copy of her remarks are below:

“Mr. Speaker, I rise today to sound the alarm about deteriorating conditions at the Eloy Detention Center.

My office has received multiple reports from the family members of people in detention and their lawyers that detainees are being denied access to proper drinking water. Instead, they are being given one cup of “ice chips” per day.

In fact, I just met with Sonya, the wife of Yari, who was diagnosed with leukemia and is currently being held at Eloy.

Her wife told her that detainees are only being given ice chips for water, which they have to wait until they melt.

Two housing blocks are also without air conditioning.

This is an outrage.

At least 57 people have already died in ICE custody this year – 4 of them in Arizona. This number is likely higher. How many more human beings need to die before we do something?

This is a moral failure. I’m calling on DHS to immediately address these conditions and ensure that all detainees have access to safe drinking water, edible food, and humane living conditions.”

title: A días del noveno aniversario de María, Hernández, Thompson y Pou presentan proyecto para dar más tiempo a Puerto Rico para terminar la reconstrucción
text:
WASHINGTON, DC — A días de cumplirse nueve años del huracán María, el comisionado residente Pablo José Hernández, junto al demócrata de mayor rango del Comité de Seguridad Nacional de la Cámara de Representantes, Bennie Thompson (MS-02), y la representante Nellie Pou (NJ-09), presentó al H.R. 10441 - Puerto Rico Disaster Recovery Completion Act of 2026, para dar a Puerto Rico hasta 2035 para completar proyectos elegibles de recuperación financiados por FEMA y evitar que las fechas límite federales se conviertan en otro obstáculo para terminar la reconstrucción.

“Agilizar la reconstrucción es parte de nuestra agenda para priorizar lo básico. Tenemos un problema: los fondos para ciertos proyectos tienen fecha de expiración y hay que pedir extensiones para cada uno. Eso toma tiempo y aumenta la carga burocrática. Por eso proponemos una extensión para todos los proyectos hasta 2035”.

“Sin lugar a dudas, Puerto Rico debe contar con todas las herramientas que necesita para poder reconstruirse tras el huracán María, un desastre devastador que la administración Trump manejó mal desde el principio. La recuperación de Puerto Rico no debe verse obstaculizada por plazos ni trabas burocráticas que dificulten completar la recuperación de la isla”, añadió el miembro de mayor rango Thompson. “Puerto Rico debe contar con el tiempo que necesita para reconstruirse por completo, y agradezco al comisionado residente Hernández por presentar esta legislación.”

“Como una de los pocos miembros puertorriqueños del Congreso, asumo con gran seriedad nuestra responsabilidad con la isla y su gente. Esta legislación dará a nuestros conciudadanos estadounidenses el tiempo y la flexibilidad que necesitan para recuperarse plenamente”, dijo la congresista Pou (Traducción del inglés). “Ahora mismo, en 2026, hay familias que dependen de cargar agua de pozos para beber y lavar su ropa. La red eléctrica continúa en condiciones críticas. Nuestro gobierno federal debe dar a los puertorriqueños todas las herramientas y el tiempo que necesitan para recuperarse plenamente. Este proyecto de ley es un primer paso clave.”

“En Mayagüez hemos vivido de primera mano lo complejo que ha sido llevar adelante los proyectos de reconstrucción. Hay procesos de permisos, revisiones, contrataciones y otras gestiones que requieren coordinación con distintas agencias y que no siempre están bajo el control de los municipios. Darle a Puerto Rico hasta 2035 nos permitiría completar proyectos que ya tienen fondos asignados, sin perder la fiscalización ni los requisitos federales. Por eso respaldo esta medida y la gestión del Comisionado Residente para que podamos terminar la reconstrucción que nuestro pueblo todavía necesita.” dijo Jorge Luis Ramos Ruiz, Alcalde de Mayagüez.

A días del noveno aniversario del huracán María, la reconstrucción de Puerto Rico sigue inconclusa. Al 30 de septiembre de 2025, COR3 reportó 19,202 proyectos activos de recuperación relacionados con María que ya tenían fondos obligados, pero que todavía no habían llegado a su cierre, una muestra de la magnitud del trabajo que queda pendiente casi una década después del huracán.

COR3 ha identificado entre los cuellos de botella los complejos requisitos federales, los procesos de permisos y revisión ambiental, las limitaciones de mano de obra y de la cadena de suministros, y los retos de coordinación entre las entidades locales y federales, factores que continúan retrasando el paso de fondos obligados a proyectos completados.

Esos atrasos fueron precisamente lo que el Comisionado Residente junto a los Congresistas Thompson y Pou examinaron este verano durante una delegación del Comité de Seguridad Nacional (Homeland Security) de la Cámara de Representantes a Puerto Rico. Los miembros se reunieron con funcionarios de FEMA, alcaldes y líderes locales para escuchar directamente los obstáculos que enfrenta la reconstrucción y visitaron proyectos como la Escuela Superior Francisco Morales en Naranjito, donde la reconstrucción permanente no comenzó hasta años después de María.

Puerto Rico todavía tiene proyectos de reconstrucción de FEMA sin completar, pero esos proyectos no tienen una sola fecha límite común. Cada obra tiene su propio plazo de ejecución y, cuando no puede terminarse a tiempo, el Gobierno tiene que solicitar una extensión a FEMA proyecto por proyecto.

El Puerto Rico Disaster Recovery Completion Act of 2026 responde directamente a ese problema al extender hasta el 31 de diciembre de 2035 el periodo de ejecución y la fecha límite para completar los proyectos de recuperación de FEMA cubiertos por la medida. Esto daría más tiempo para terminar proyectos elegibles, mientras obliga a FEMA a informar qué obras continúan pendientes, qué obstáculos están provocando atrasos y cuándo se espera que sean completadas.

La legislación:

Extendería hasta el 31 de diciembre de 2035 el plazo para completar proyectos elegibles de obras permanentes de FEMA que todavía no hayan llegado a su cierre;

Permitiría solicitar extensiones adicionales después de 2035 mediante el proceso existente de FEMA cuando sea necesario;

Cubriría proyectos elegibles relacionados con los huracanes Irma y María, los terremotos de 2019-2020 y el huracán Fiona; y

Requeriría que FEMA, en consulta con COR3, presente informes anuales al Congreso y al Comisionado Residente detallando cuántos proyectos se han completado, cuándo se espera completar los que siguen en curso y qué obstáculos están retrasando las obras.

Este requisito de informes permanecería vigente hasta el 31 de diciembre de 2035, dando al Congreso una evaluación anual del progreso de los proyectos de recuperación cubiertos por la medida en Puerto Rico.

###

Nine Years After María, Hernández, Thompson and Pou Introduce Bill to Give Puerto Rico More Time to Finish Reconstruction

Hernandez’s legislation would provide Puerto Rico until 2035 to complete eligible disaster recovery projects and require FEMA to report on obstacles and timelines.

WASHINGTON, DC — As Puerto Rico approaches the ninth anniversary of Hurricane María, Resident Commissioner Pablo José Hernández of Puerto Rico alongside House Homeland Security Committee Ranking Member Bennie Thompson (MS-02) and Representative Nellie Pou (NJ-09) introduced H.R. 10441 - Puerto Rico Disaster Recovery Completion Act of 2026 to give Puerto Rico until 2035 to complete eligible FEMA-funded recovery projects and prevent federal deadlines from standing in the way of finishing the reconstruction.

“Nine years after María, Puerto Rico should be talking about a reconstruction completed, not deadlines that could get in the way of finishing it,” said Resident Commissioner Hernández. “Our communities have waited long enough. This bill gives Puerto Rico the time to finish the work while making sure FEMA remains accountable for getting these projects across the finish line.”

“Without question, Puerto Rico should be given all the tools it needs to be able to rebuild after Hurricane María, a devastating disaster that the Trump administration mismanaged from the very beginning. Puerto Rico’s recovery should not be hindered by deadlines and red tape that get in the way of finishing the island’s recovery,” added Ranking Member Thompson. “Puerto Rico should have the time it needs to fully rebuild, and I thank Resident Commissioner Hernández for introducing this legislation.”

“As one of the few Puerto Rican members of Congress, I take our responsibility to the island and its people very seriously. This legislation will give our fellow Americans the time and flexibility they need to make themselves whole,” said Congresswoman Pou. “Right now, in 2026, families are relying on carrying water from wells to drink and wash their clothes. The power grid remains in dire shape. Our federal government must give Puerto Ricans all of the tools and time they need to become whole again. This bill is a key start.”

“In Mayagüez, we have experienced firsthand how complex it has been to move reconstruction projects forward. There are permitting processes, reviews, contracting requirements, and other steps that require coordination with different agencies and are not always within the municipalities’ control. Giving Puerto Rico until 2035 would allow us to complete projects that already have funding allocated, without sacrificing oversight or federal requirements. That is why I support this measure and the Resident Commissioner’s efforts to ensure that we can finish the reconstruction our people still need,” said Jorge Luis Ramos Ruiz, Mayor of Mayagüez.

BACKGROUND

Ahead of the ninth anniversary of Hurricane María, Puerto Rico’s reconstruction remains unfinished. As of September 30, 2025, COR3 reported 19,202 active María recovery projects that had been obligated but had not yet reached closeout, underscoring the scale of work still underway nearly a decade after the storm. COR3 has pointed to complex federal requirements, permitting and environmental reviews, workforce and supply-chain limitations, and coordination challenges as continuing bottlenecks slowing projects from obligation to completion.

Those challenges were front and center this summer when Hernández, Thompson and Pou traveled to Puerto Rico as part of a House Homeland Security Committee delegation, where they met with FEMA officials, mayors and local leaders and visited projects such as Francisco Morales High School in Naranjito, where permanent reconstruction did not begin until years after María.

Puerto Rico still has FEMA-funded reconstruction projects that remain unfinished, but those projects do not share a single common deadline. Each project has its own completion timeline, and when it cannot be finished on time, the government must request an extension from FEMA on a project-by-project basis.

The Puerto Rico Disaster Recovery Completion Act of 2026 responds directly to those concerns by extending the period of performance and project completion deadline for covered FEMA disaster recovery projects in Puerto Rico through December 31, 2035, giving eligible projects more time to be completed while requiring FEMA to account for what remains unfinished, what is causing delays and when those projects are expected to be finished.

The legislation would:

Extend the completion deadline to December 31, 2035 for eligible FEMA permanent-work projects that have not yet been closed out;

Allow additional extensions after 2035 through FEMA’s existing extension process when more time is necessary;

Cover eligible projects stemming from Hurricanes Irma and María, the 2019-2020 earthquakes and Hurricane Fiona; and

Require FEMA, in consultation with COR3, to report annually to Congress and the Resident Commissioner on the number of projects completed, expected completion dates for projects still underway and obstacles delaying their completion.

The reporting requirement would remain in place through December 31, 2035, providing Congress with an annual accounting of the progress of covered recovery projects in Puerto Rico.

title: President Trump Signs Hudson Bill to Complete National EMS Memorial Into Law
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Last week, U.S. Representative Richard Hudson’s (NC-09) applauded President Donald Trump’s signature into law of his legislation to complete the National Emergency Medical Services Memorial in Washington, D.C. The bipartisan law gives the National Emergency Medical Services Memorial Foundation more time to complete the memorial at no cost to the taxpayer.

“Each year, 850,000 EMS professionals respond to more than 30 million calls for assistance. It’s time we finally give these unsung heroes the recognition they deserve,” said Rep. Hudson. “I’m grateful President Trump signed my bill into law so we can honor their service with a permanent memorial in our nation’s capital.”

Hudson’s legislation is a clean, bipartisan extension. Congress first authorized the memorial in 2018, but that authority expired under the Commemorative Works Act before the project could be completed. The new law extends the authorization for an additional seven years from enactment, giving the Foundation time to complete approvals and private fundraising so the memorial can move forward.

Background

In 2018, Congress authorized the National Emergency Medical Services Memorial Foundation to establish a commemorative work in Washington, D.C., honoring EMS professionals. Under the Commemorative Works Act, that authority expires after seven years unless extended.

EMS personnel are often the first to respond in moments of crisis, including natural disasters like hurricanes in North Carolina, accidents, and public health emergencies. Despite their service and sacrifice, there is still no permanent memorial in the nation’s capital honoring EMS professionals who lost their lives in the line of duty.

The Department of the Interior supported Hudson’s legislation, which passed the House unanimously with bipartisan support before being signed into law by President Trump.

title: Ranking Members Jared Huffman, Robert Garcia, and Gregory Meeks Demand Answers on Trump Administration’s Oil Deal with Alleged Money Launderer
text:

Gregory W. Meeks, Ranking Member of the Committee on Foreign Affairs demanded answers from Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Attorney General Todd Blanche on how they sprung alleged white collar criminal Alejandro Betancourt to lead the Trump Administration’s unprecedented scheme to take an ownership stake in a Venezuelan oil company.

"Handing a stake in another nation’s oil wealth to a man under active criminal investigation for money laundering is exactly how the Trump administration does business. Americans are paying more at the pump while the President’s war of choice in Iran drags on, and instead of bringing relief, this White House cut a deal that appears to reward corruption. Rubio and Blanche owe Congress a full account of what they did to get Alejandro Betancourt off the hook and why. Democrats will keep demanding those answers until the American people get the truth,” said Ranking Member Huffman.

“The Trump Administration’s Venezuelan oil takeover now involves going into business with Alejandro Betancourt, an alleged money launderer who is under active criminal investigation. While President Trump’s war in Iran continues to drive up prices, it appears this Administration may have pressured foreign governments to release yet another person surrounded by corruption,” said Ranking Member Robert Garcia.

“The administration owes the American and Venezuelan people answers for why Alejandro Betancourt—known for alleged corruption and money-laundering in Venezuela and elsewhere—is being treated as a business partner instead of the subject of a law enforcement investigation. Partnering with Betancourt on this shady oil deal suggests that Trump and Rubio remain more focused on pillaging Venezuela for its natural resources to the benefit of their friends and donors than on a democratic transition there. Both the American and Venezuelan people deserve better,” said Ranking Member Gregory W. Meeks.

In the letter to Secretary Rubio and Attorney General Blanche, Ranking Members Garcia, Meeks, and Huffman wrote, “Despite previous promises of transparency and repeated requests from Congress, the Trump Administration has provided shockingly few details to Congress regarding its management of at least $13 billion in Venezuelan oil revenue. Last week, President Trump announced an unprecedented financial takeover of another country’s natural resources, in a partnership deal between the U.S. government and North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), a private company led by Venezuelan businessman and alleged money launderer Alejandro Betancourt. Given the numerous corruption allegations surrounding Mr. Betancourt, we demand information on the negotiations that led to this deal. We also demand information about the steps the Department of State and Department of Justice (DOJ) took to pressure a foreign government to resolve an active investigation into Mr. Betancourt’s activities, including your personal involvements as Secretary of State and Attorney General.”

In August 2026, Ranking Member Robert Garcia escalated Oversight Democrats’ investigation into the Departments of Treasury, State, and Energy regarding their roles in managing Venezuelan oil revenue after launching the probe in February 2026. In January 2026, Ranking Member Garcia demanded answers from oil trading companies Vitol and Trafigura regarding their role in the Trump Administration’s sale of Venezuelan oil and any agreements made between the companies and the Administration. In January 2026, Ranking Member Garcia and every Oversight Democrat demanded answers on any communication from the Trump Administration with major oil companies Chevron, ExxonMobil, ConocoPhillips, and Continental Resources regarding the Trump Administration’s military action against Venezuela and the President’s plan to seize the country’s oil wealth.

title: Jayapal, Wilson, Booker Introduce Legislation to Combat High Rate of Heart Disease in South Asian Americans
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Representatives Pramila Jayapal (WA-07) and Joe Wilson (SC-02) and U.S. Senator Cory Booker (D-NJ) are reintroducing the bipartisan South Asian Heart Health Awareness and Research Act, landmark legislation to both raise awareness about the alarming rate of heart disease for South Asians across the United States and put resources and strategies toward reversing this deadly trend for all communities.

“As the first South Asian American woman ever elected to the House of Representatives, I’m fully committed to increasing understanding of heart disease and the unique risk factors in the South Asian community while ensuring that all those living with it get the resources, treatment, and support they need,” said Rep. Jayapal. “Heart disease has been the leading cause of death for over a century, and it is even more dire in the South Asian community. The South Asian Heart Health Awareness and Research Act is essential legislation that ensures that we have the research, resources, and treatments to prevent heart disease cases and deaths in the South Asian community and beyond.”

“Heart disease disproportionately affects certain populations such as the South Asian community, and this bill will expand research and education to benefit those communities. I am grateful that this bipartisan bill passed the House in multiple previous Congresses, and I look forward to its final passage into law,” said Rep. Joe Wilson.

“Heart disease is taking South Asian Americans from their families at rates the medical community still doesn’t fully understand,” said Senator Booker. ” This bill puts real research dollars behind the risk factors hiding in plain sight, so doctors can catch what they’ve been missing. Every community deserves to have its heart health taken seriously, not treated as an afterthought.”

Studies show that South Asians in the United States – people who immigrated from or whose families immigrated from countries including India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Nepal – are experiencing a dramatic rise in heart disease and face four times the risk of heart disease compared to the general population. Despite making up 25 percent of the world’s population, South Asians account for a disproportionate 60 percent of the world’s heart disease cases and over 50 percent of the world’s cardiovascular deaths. Almost two-thirds of middle-aged South Asian Americans are at intermediate or high risk for heart failure within the next 10 years, and because research agencies within the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) do not disaggregate medical data for Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders, it is nearly impossible to examine data on South Asian Americans.

Heart disease is widely prevalent in the United States, but is not well understood. One person in America dies every 34 seconds from cardiovascular disease, and costs associated with heart disease in the United States — including indirect costs — exceed $500 billion annually and is projected to surpass $1 trillion by 2035.

The South Asian Heart Health Awareness and Research Act would authorize the HHS Secretary to make grants available to states to promote awareness of the increasing prevalence of heart disease in South Asian communities. These grants can be used to:

Develop culturally appropriate materials on topics such as nutrition education, optimal diet plans, and programs for regular exercise.

Support heart health promotion activities of community organizations that work with or serve communities disproportionately affected by heart disease.

Support conferences or workshops on research practices, methodology, and design to include more members of communities disproportionately affected by heart disease in scientific studies.

The legislation also directs the HHS Secretary to submit a report to Congress on the grant activities and any data gathered related to heart disease in disproportionately impacted communities and authorizes funding for these programs through 2028.

“South Asian Americans have faced a disproportionate burden of cardiovascular disease for far too long, while gaps in data, research, and culturally responsive prevention continue to limit our ability to address it. The South Asian Heart Health Awareness and Research Act is an important commitment to changing that by investing in the evidence and community-based public health efforts needed to prevent disease and improve outcomes. SAPHA has supported this legislation for years, and we urge lawmakers to support the South Asian Heart Health Awareness and Research Act and its efforts to expand culturally appropriate heart health education and prevention, strengthen community-based outreach, and improve research on cardiovascular disease in South Asian communities,” said Samira Khan, MPH, CHES President, South Asian Public Health Association (SAPHA)

The South Asian Heart Health Awareness and Research Act is sponsored by representatives Nanette Barragán (CA-44), Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-01), Henry Johnson (GA-04), Ro Khanna (CA-17), Adam Smith (WA-09), Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10) and Shri Thanedar (MI-13).

The legislation has been endorsed by the American Heart Association, the Asian Pacific American Medical Student Association (APAMSA), El Camino Health, Indian American Impact, MASALA Study, the National Asian Pacific American Women’s Forum, the South Asian Health Initiative (SAHELI) and the South Asian Public Health Association (SAPHA).

title: LEADER JEFFRIES STATEMENT ON THE RISE OF ANTI-SOUTH ASIAN HATE
text:
Today, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries released the following statement:

title: Ranking Members Larson, Neal, and Davis Demand Answers from Commissioner Bisignano for Social Security Staffing Crisis
text:
Washington, D.C. - Today, House Social Security Subcommittee Ranking Member John B. Larson (CT-01), Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E. Neal (MA-01), and Worker and Family Support Subcommittee Ranking Member Danny K. Davis (IL-07) wrote to Social Security Administration (SSA) Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano, demanding answers for the staffing crisis at SSA taking hold on his watch—after delivering seemingly contradictory testimony before the Ways and Means Committee earlier this year.

During his testimony, Commissioner Bisignano asserted that SSA has “the right amount of staff in the right places,” that they’ve “reduced workload in field offices by the equivalent of 600 work years,” and that “we committed to never close a field office.” However, reports by the American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) Council 220, representing approximately 25,000 SSA employees, contradict him. The union told Congress that severely understaffed field offices are operating as “ghost offices” and record-low morale have created the worst staffing crisis in SSA’s history. The union noted that the Administration has forced out roughly one in seven SSA employees nationwide.

“During the hearing, you testified that you are delivering ‘the best all-around performance ever at the Social Security Administration,’” the Democratic lawmakers wrote. “Unfortunately, the experience on the ground as reported by our constituents and as highlighted by AFGE Council 220 in its statement contradicts this testimony.”

The lawmakers requested Commissioner Bisignano answer by October 2, 2026, for the crisis afoot amidst an effort to “trample on the rights of unionized employees.” The questions probe the changes in SSA’s workplace policy, criteria used to reassign employees and its effect on customer service, and canceling of previously agreed upon employee accommodations. The Democrats demanded to know what notice is given to SSA employees regarding changes to their employment, and what steps are taken to ensure reasonable accommodation and Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) requests.

title: Bipartisan Coalition Introduce Resolution Designating “National Adult Education and Family Literacy Week”
text:
Resolution promotes adult foundational education, workforce development, and family literacy programs

Washington, DC – Representatives Lucy McBath (GA-06), Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-01), Frank Mrvan (D-IN-01), and Ryan Mackenzie (PA-07) have introduced H.Res.1550 designating September 13th through September 19th of 2026 as “National Adult Education and Family Literacy Week.” The resolution is led in the Senate by U.S. Senators Jack Reed (D-RI) and Susan Collins (R-ME). It recognizes the importance of adult education, family literacy, and efforts to support an educated population with the literacy skills necessary to succeed in the 21st century.

“Education is the key to opportunity. Our goal is to give all Americans, no matter their age, the chance to create the best possible lives for themselves,” said Rep. McBath. “Low literacy and numeracy rates among adults hinder opportunities not only for themselves, but for their children. By recognizing National Adult Education and Family Literacy Week, we are highlighting the need for increased investment in initiatives that help adults build the skills they need to be successful.”

“Adult education and family literacy are the gateway to opportunity, dignity, and a stronger workforce,” said Rep. Fitzpatrick. “By investing in foundational skills, workforce readiness, and family literacy, we’re closing gaps and unlocking potential. This bipartisan resolution reaffirms our commitment to every adult learner striving for a better future, equipping parents to guide the next generation, strengthening our communities, and securing a more competitive, resilient America for decades to come.”

“Thank you to Rep. McBath and my House colleagues for this bipartisan resolution to support National Adult Education and Family Literacy Week. Let us continue to advocate for more life-long educational opportunities that improve literacy rates and empower individuals across the country to thrive in the workforce and succeed in our economy,” said Rep. Mrvan.

“Adult education and family literacy programs help people build the skills they need to succeed,” said Rep. Mackenzie. To highlight the importance of these programs, I’m joining Rep. Lucy McBath and other colleagues in recognizing National Adult Education and Family Literacy Week. Learning is a lifelong activity, and this resolution highlights the importance of literacy for our families, workforce, and communities.”

Background

Nearly 59,000,000 adults in the United States struggle with basic literacy; 72,000,000 struggle with numeracy, and one-third of the U.S. adult population struggles with multi-step problem-solving which limits effective decision-making in everyday life. These same individuals experience higher unemployment rates and lower wages, making it harder for them to support their families.Adult education helps Americans gain the skills they need to become employed, advance in their jobs, engage in postsecondary and training programs, and achieve economic self-sufficiency.

The importance of having these skills also extends into life at home. Parental duties among American adults account for a significant portion of the education of our future generation. Whether it is the practice of reading to their child or teaching them everyday skills for later in life, increased parental involvement is a consistent indicator of success for that child later in life.

The resolution will:

Raise public awareness about the importance of adult education, workforce skills, and family literacy.

Encourage people across the United States to support programs that assist individuals in need of adult education, workforce skills, and family literacy programs.

Recognize the importance of these programs.

Call on public, private, and nonprofit entities to support increased access to adult education and family literacy programs to ensure a fully literate society.

title: Maryland Congressional Delegation Members Announce Over $30 Million for Infrastructure Upgrades at Maryland Airports
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Representatives April McClain Delaney, Sarah Elfreth, and Johnny Olszewski and U.S. Senators Chris Van Hollen and Angela Alsobrooks (all D-Md.) announced $33,931,039 in federal funding to support infrastructure and equipment upgrades at Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI), Carroll County Regional Airport, and Hagerstown Regional Airport. The investments will fund important safety improvements at all three airports, as well as upgraded equipment and an evaluation of the noise exposure at BWI, including its impact on surrounding communities, which members of Maryland’s Congressional Delegation urged the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to address in April.

"Maryland’s airports and aviation industry are crucial for trade and business. Thanks to the hard work of Team Maryland, our congressional offices secured more than $30 million to make our airports safer, more accessible, and more efficient. These investments will provide Hagerstown Regional Airport with the funds necessary to make improvements to its 2/20 runway and adjacent building infrastructure—critical safety upgrades needed to fully comply with FAA guidance,” said Congresswoman McClain Delaney.

“Maryland’s airports are economic engines, serving travelers and businesses across the region and around the world. That’s why we worked to deliver these investments in important updates to BWI, Carroll County Regional, and Hagerstown Regional airports. These federal funds will help ensure these airports meet important safety standards, and, at BWI, will support efforts to address local communities’ noise concerns,” said Senator Van Hollen.

“Our airports here in Maryland fuel our economy, connect us to the rest of the world, and support our businesses. I am proud to partner with my colleagues to announce over $33 million in federal funding to upgrade the infrastructure at three of our airports. Modernizing our infrastructure is an investment in our future and in our safety – I’m glad we are getting this done,” said Senator Alsobrooks.

“Airports are not simply places where flights arrive and depart – they are engines of opportunity, connecting people to jobs, businesses to customers, communities to global markets, and regions to long-term economic growth,” said Congresswoman Sarah Elfreth. “Each of Maryland’s airports, including the Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport here in the Third Congressional District, has played a critical role in the growth of our communities, our state, and our nation. I was grateful to work with Team Maryland to secure this much-needed $21 million investment for BWI that will evaluate noise exposure for our neighbors and ensure the safety of worldwide travelers,” said Congresswoman Elfreth.

“As Maryland continues to grow, we must ensure our airports have the infrastructure and equipment they need to operate safely, efficiently, and effectively,” said Congressman Olszewski. “This funding will strengthen our aviation infrastructure and help ensure these facilities can continue serving our communities and the rest of the nation. I was proud to work with Team Maryland to help deliver these critical investments.”

The federal funding has been announced as follows:

$21,091,172 to Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI) to support an evaluation of noise exposure at the airport and surrounding areas as well as the reconstruction of 110,000 square yards of the existing North Cargo Apron pavement and installation of low-emission equipment, including five gate electrification systems and remote ground power units.

$7,609,500 to Carroll County Regional Airport to shift Runway 16/34 by 250 feet to bring the airport into conformity with current standards.

$5,230,367 to Hagerstown Regional Airport to remove a building and relocate fencing identified as obstructive by the Federal Aviation Administration. The funding will also help the airport rehabilitate lighting and 3000 feet of pavement on Runway 2/20 to maintain the structural integrity and minimize foreign object debris.

These investments are provided through the FAA’s Airport Improvement Program (AIP). Senator Van Hollen worked to fund the AIP through the passage of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, which authorized $4 billion a year for Fiscal Years 2025 through 2028.

title: Rep. McDonald Rivet, Democratic Women’s Caucus Call on HHS to Withdraw Dangerous Plan to Overhaul Head Start
text:
WASHINGTON— Congresswoman Kristen McDonald Rivet (MI-08) and the Democratic Women’s Caucus (DWC) sent a letter, calling on the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to withdraw a proposed rule slashing 90% of Head Start Program Performance Standards, which would harm Head Start children, families, and classrooms.

“Head Start makes sure children from low-income families and children with disabilities have a loving place to learn and grow. There are decades of research proving Head Start kids do better in school and better in life,” said Congresswoman McDonald Rivet. “This Administration’s proposed overhaul will wreak havoc on what makes Head Start so special. It’ll make it harder for kids to learn, harder for teachers to do their jobs, and harder for working parents to make ends meet. We can’t let it go forward.”

For over 60 years, Head Start has provided child care and social services for children from low-income families, children with disabilities, dual language learners, and children experiencing homelessness. HHS’s proposed rule would eliminate over 1,400 regulatory provisions and largely defer rules and guidelines to states and local programs. These changes would severely diminish the quality of Head Start services, including:

Weakening protections for children with disabilities.

Eliminating federal limits on class size and staff-to-student ratios.

Rolling back credential requirements for Head Start staff and teachers.

Reducing health and safety protections for children.

Cutting program hours.

Leading the letter alongside Congresswoman McDonald Rivet are DWC Chair Teresa Leger Fernández (NM-03) and DWC Members Debbie Dingell (MI-06), Brittany Pettersen (CO-07), and Lateefah Simon (CA-12). 70 Members of Congress signed the letter.

The letter from the lawmakers reads, in part, “This proposed rule guts an essential early childhood program and its services for hundreds of thousands of women and families nationwide, which would increase their costs and burden to replace those services. In today’s environment of rising costs, it is cruel to make life more difficult and expensive for these families.”

A copy of the letter can be found here.

Prior to serving in elected office, Congresswoman McDonald Rivet served as Executive Director of Michigan Head Start.

title: McGovern, Merkley, Duckworth, Walkinshaw Urge Trump Administration: Do Not Deport People Back to Persecution and Torture in China
text:
Lawmakers Make Letter Public So Attorneys Can Use It to Support At-Risk Uyghur, Hong Konger, Tibetan and Chinese Asylum Seekers Held in ICE Detention

WASHINGTON—Yesterday, Representative James P. McGovern (D-MA), Ranking Member of the House Rules Committee and the Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC), along with Senators Jeff Merkley (D-OR) and Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) and Representative James R. Walkinshaw (D-VA), sent a letter to Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling on the Trump Administration to protect people who have fled repression in China and could face persecution or torture if they are sent back.

McGovern, Merkley, Duckworth, and Walkinshaw all serve on the CECC—a congressional commission that monitors and documents human rights violations in the People’s Republic of China (PRC).

In the letter, the lawmakers called on the U.S. government to stop the practice of detaining at-risk individuals, release those currently in detention, prohibit them from being deported to the PRC, and give fair and timely consideration of their applications for asylum.

“Many people who have fled persecution in the PRC come to the United States with an expectation that they can find refuge,” the Members wrote. “They should be given every opportunity to apply for asylum if they have not yet done so and given fair and timely consideration of such application for asylum or other protection. Under no circumstances should at-risk individuals be deported to the PRC.”

The Members also made the letter public so immigration attorneys and advocates can use it in cases involving Uyghurs, Hong Kongers, Tibetans and others who fear persecution if returned to China.

“There are likely many more detainees at ICE facilities, perhaps lacking representation, who fear deportation to a country run by a government that seeks to do them harm,” the Members continued. “There are perhaps others who have already been sent back to the PRC who are now experiencing persecution, torture or worse. Thus, we see value in making this letter and its message public.”

The letter notes that the U.S. government deporting an individual to a country where their life or freedom would be threatened (also known as “refoulement”) would violate both United States and international law, and would also be a betrayal of that promise by then-Senator Marco Rubio to provide refuge to those subject to the repression of the Chinese Communist Party, when he introduced the Hong Kong Safe Harbor Act and the Uyghur Human Rights Protection Act.

The full text of the letter is available here.

title: Meuser Commends President Trump for Extending Most Favored Nation Drug Pricing to All State Medicaid Programs
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, Congressman Dan Meuser (PA-09) released the following statement commending President Donald Trump, Secretary of Health Robert Kennedy Jr., and Administrator Mehmet Oz on rolling out Most Favored Nation (MFN) drug pricing to Medicaid beneficiaries in all 50 states.

Last May, President Trump signed an executive order requiring pharmaceutical manufacturers to offer their products in the United States at the same low price offered in other nations. Since then, the Trump Administration has secured agreements with 26 major pharmaceutical companies to offer nearly 90% of branded pharmaceutical products on the market at MFN pricing. The deals cover a variety of drugs and deliver significant cost reductions, including an 88% decrease in the cost of multiple sclerosis medication, a 90% decrease in the cost of Hepatitis C medication, and an 81% decrease in the cost of diabetes medicines.

So far, MFN pricing has been accessible to consumers via TrumpRx, which connects consumers directly to pharmaceutical companies to purchase prescription drugs at MFN pricing. Today’s announcement expands MFN pricing to Medicaid beneficiaries in all 50 states through the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation GENEROUS Model, which requires manufacturers to provide supplemental rebates to states to align Medicaid drug prices with what other countries pay. The Council of Economic Advisors estimates that today’s announcement will save Medicaid a total of $64.3 billion over the next decade. The federal government would save $36.6 billion, while the states would save the remaining $27.6 billion.

“Today’s announcement marks an important milestone in expanding Most Favored Nation drug pricing to Americans nationwide,” said Congressman Meuser. “Pennsylvanians who are on Medicaid will now see a substantial reduction in their drug pricing due to the policies of the Trump Administration. We can continue to build on this success by passing my Most Favored Patient Act, which would lock in MFN savings for years to come and ensure that all Americans can purchase drugs at lower prices.”

Congressman Meuser’s Work on Lower Drug Prices:

Congressman Meuser has led the effort in Congress to codify the MFN drug pricing deals that the Trump Administration has secured through the Most Favored Patient Act. This legislation would codify the 26 existing MFN drug pricing deals and establish a permanent framework to codify and enforce future cost-saving healthcare agreements as they are reached. This legislation would lock in at least $600 billion in savings for the American people.

During last year’s State of the Union Address, President Trump called on Congress to codify the existing MFN and included it in his Great Healthcare Plan, which would lower drug prices and premiums for all Americans.

title: Rep. Min Leads 31 Colleagues in Demanding Answers on University Research Funding Cuts
text:
Washington, DC. — Congressman Dave Min (CA-47) led 31 colleagues in pressing the White House for answers on reported disruptions to congressionally appropriated federal research funding, warning that cuts, delays, and funding shifts at federal science agencies target colleges and universities that have long helped drive American research, innovation, and technological leadership.

In a letter to the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) and Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP), the members raised concerns over reports that the Trump administration is withholding or redirecting federal research funding and shifting resources away from institutions of higher education. The members requested a briefing and written answers on any involvement by OMB or OSTP in changes to Fiscal Year 2026 research funding, including funds that have been withheld, reprogrammed, or reduced and the legal authority underlying those actions.

“Universities are critical to the advancement of research that drives innovation and develops the next generation of scientific talent,” the members wrote. “Abruptly shifting resources away from established research programs undermines the stability of the nation’s innovation ecosystem and is already having negative repercussions on university campuses. Delays and uncertainty in NSF and NIH research funding are forcing schools to reduce critical Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics facilities, programs, and experts, pause the hiring of new postdoctoral and graduate students, and re-evaluate long-standing technology transfer partnerships with industry. These disruptions not only threaten the United States’s ability to recruit, train, and retain the next generation of innovators, but also research that serves as the foundation for future discoveries.”

These developments come as OSTP has outlined a broader effort to restructure how the federal government supports scientific research. In its July report, Science: A New Golden Age, OSTP recommended refocusing federal support on individual scientists rather than “legacy institutions,” expanding alternative funding models, and creating new research organizations such as X-Labs. The White House has directed federal research and development agencies to develop plans to implement the report’s recommendations.

The requested information includes, where applicable:

Any advice, direction, or consultation by OSTP or OMB with NSF, NIH, or any other federal science agency regarding reductions, reprogramming, or other changes to Fiscal Year 2026 research funding, including the nature of those communications, identify the agencies involved, and any recommendations or directives issued by OSTP or OMB.

All Fiscal Year 2026 funding for NSF, NIH, and other federal science agencies that have been withheld, reprogrammed, or recommended for reduction following guidance or recommendations from OSTP or OMB, including the affected account or program, the amount of funding, the date of the action, the stated rationale, and the intended use of any redirected or reprogrammed funds.

The statutory authority OMB intends to rely upon to implement the recommendations outlined in OSTP’s report, Science: A New Golden Age, particularly those calling for the federal government to “fundamentally change how research dollars are allocated, distributed, and assessed” and prioritize funding for individual scientists and non-traditional research organizations over “legacy institutions.”

Any changes to existing federal grantmaking procedures or priorities being considered, planned, or have been implemented.

An explanation of how OSTP’s recommendations regarding changes to federal research funding align with congressional directives for fiscal year 2026 appropriations, including language directing NSF to equitably disburse funding across its basic research directorates and prohibiting any directorate from receiving “more than 5 percent reduction [in funding] relative to the fiscal year 2025 enacted level.”

The members requested a response and briefing no later than October 1, 2026.

title: Congressman Griffith’s Weekly E-Newsletter 9.18.26
text:
The alarming rates of maternal and infant mortality in the United States demand continued federal diligence.

Reportedly America suffers from the highest maternal and infant mortality rates in the developed world. But according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), more than 80% of our pregnancy-related deaths are preventable.

Because of my concerns about this problem, I am working with federal partners to find solutions.

One of these partners, Healthy Moms Healthy Babies America (HMHBA), which was founded in 2026 by Cara Osborne and Olivia Walton, put a meeting together of a select group of 15 officials.

Besides me, some of the others in the group included Second Lady Usha Vance, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz, Tennessee Senator Marsha Blackburn, Ohio Congressman Jim Jordan and former White House official Kellyanne Conway.

Second Lady Vance shared with us her experiences regarding her most recent pregnancy, birth and care following the birth.

One of the things she suggested was that we look at the combined medical assessments for both children and mothers.

She advocated that these visits should not be weeks after birth, but closer to when the mother and child are released from the hospital. Doing so would help identify any problems that might be developing related to either the child’s health or potential emotional issues of the mother. Telehealth can help facilitate health care provider access for the mother and child.

I recall one former client of mine who struggled with exhaustion and postpartum depression as a result of caring for newborn twins. Her condition became so severe that she had to be committed to a hospital for 48 hours to ensure her safety and well-being.

Childbirth can cause great potential for stress, exhaustion and postpartum depression, among other issues.

Second Lady Vance advocated for better monitoring of the health for moms and babies in the weeks after birth.

Dr. Oz discussed the recent rollout of the new CMS ACCESS Model. Under this program, his agency is supporting the extension of care beyond the clinic and harnessing artificial intelligence (AI) and telehealth to reach more families.

I believe telehealth and telemedicine, now coupled with technological advances, including wearables (Oura rings and Apple watches, etc.) with AI-analyzed data, will make a huge difference in the future.

These wearables can help moms track their health, spot trouble early and connect with providers before things get urgent. She can check her vitals, get advice from a nurse over video and know she’s got a team watching out for her, even if the nearest clinic is miles away.

During the same week of the HMHBA event, I held a hearing as the Health Subcommittee Chairman to consider various policies. One of the bills discussed during the hearing was the Rural Obstetric Readiness Act by Democratic Illinois Congresswoman Robin Kelly.

The Rural Obstetric Readiness Act seeks to create a new health care reality where we train more rural health providers and doctors to handle obstetric care.

The National Rural Health Association notes that more than 67% of rural counties lack hospital-based obstetrical services, with a majority of these counties lacking an obstetric clinician. That is more than double the rate of urban localities.

Accordingly, more than two million American women live in what experts call “maternity care deserts.”

The spirit of Congresswoman Kelly’s bill is to tackle maternal care deserts, which make pregnancy-related complications more dangerous for mothers and infants.

Earlier this year, I voted for the Preventing Maternal Deaths Act and Prematurity Research Expansion and Education for Mothers who Deliver Infants Early (PREEMIE) Act, which are now law. These bills help federal agencies coordinate mortality prevention activities and promote prenatal care.

Virginia state policy is treading on a path of maternal health success as well.

In 2025, a new state law took effect to allow licensed certified midwives and nurse practitioners to access pediatric privileges where they can serve on 24-hour on-call duty for nursery care when physicians are unavailable.

Having a midwife assist in areas where there are maternal care deserts will help enhance the rural health care workforce.

Taken together, these and other policy ideas can produce dividends for maternal care.

By strengthening access to maternal health resources, mothers will be in a better position to give care to their children and live healthy lives.

I will continue to work for policies that nurture an environment supporting mothers, improving maternal care and fighting to eliminate maternity care deserts.

If you have questions, concerns, or comments, feel free to contact my office. You can call my Abingdon office at 276-525-1405 or my Christiansburg office at 540-381-5671. To reach my office via email, please visit my website at https://morgangriffith.house.gov/.
